arXiv:2404.04239v3 [math.NT] 15 Jan 2026

Large sieve inequalities for exceptional Maass forms and the greatest prime factor of n2+1n^{2}+1

Alexandru Pascadi Address: Mathematisches Institut, Endenicher Allee 60, 53115 Bonn, Germany Email address: alexpascadi@gmail.com
Abstract.

We prove new large sieve inequalities for the Fourier coefficients ρj​𝔞​(n)\rho_{j\mathfrak{a}}(n) of exceptional Maass forms of a given level, weighted by sequences (an)(a_{n}) with sparse Fourier transforms—including two key types of sequences that arise in the dispersion method. These give the first savings in the exceptional spectrum for the critical case of sequences as long as the level, and lead to improved bounds for various multilinear forms of Kloosterman sums.

As an application, we show that the greatest prime factor of n2+1n^{2}+1 is infinitely often greater than n1.3n^{1.3}, improving Merikoski’s previous threshold of n1.279n^{1.279}. We also announce applications to the exponents of distribution of primes and smooth numbers in arithmetic progressions.

1. Introduction

Let m,n,c∈ℤm,n,c\in\mathbb{Z} with c≥1c\geq 1, and consider the classical Kloosterman sums

(1.1) S⁡(m,n,c):=∑x∈(ℤ/c​ℤ)×e⁡(m​x+n​x¯c),S(m,n;c):=\sum_{x\in(\mathbb{Z}/c\mathbb{Z})^{\times}}e\left(\frac{mx+n\overline{x}}{c}\right),

where e⁡(α):=exp⁡(2​π​i​α)e(\alpha):=\exp(2\pi i\alpha) and x​x¯≡1​(mod ​c)x\overline{x}\equiv 1\ (\textnormal{mod }c). A great number of results in analytic number theory, particularly on the distribution of primes [2, 34, 35, 36, 10, 8, 37, 32] and properties of Dirichlet LL-functions [11, 12, 46, 48, 15, 45], rely on bounding exponential sums of the form

(1.2) ∑m∼Mam​∑n∼Nbn​∑(c,r)=1g⁡(cC)​S​(m​r¯,±n,s​c),\sum_{m\sim M}a_{m}\sum_{n\sim N}b_{n}\sum_{(c,r)=1}g\left(\frac{c}{C}\right)S(m\overline{r},\pm n;sc),

where (am)(a_{m}) and (bn)(b_{n}) are rough sequences of complex numbers, gg is a compactly-supported smooth function, and r,sr,s are coprime positive integers. One can often (but not always [37, 8, 34]) leverage some additional averaging over rr and ss, if one of the sequences (am),(bn)(a_{m}),(b_{n}) is independent of r,sr,s.

Estimates for sums like 1.2 are typically obtained via the spectral theory of automorphic forms [25, 24], following Deshouillers–Iwaniec [9]; this allows one to bound 1.2 by certain averages of the sequences (am)(a_{m}), (bn)(b_{n}) with the Fourier coefficients of automorphic forms for Γ0​(r​s)\Gamma_{0}(rs). Often in applications, the limitation in these bounds comes from our inability to rule out the existence of exceptional Maass cusp forms, corresponding to exceptional eigenvalues λ∈(0,14)\lambda\in(0,\tfrac{1}{4}) of the hyperbolic Laplacian. This is measured by a parameter θ=maxλ⁡max⁡(0,14−λ)1/2\theta=\max_{\lambda}\max(0,\tfrac{1}{4}-\lambda)^{1/2}; under Selberg’s eigenvalue conjecture there would be no exceptional eigenvalues [41], so one could take θ=0\theta=0. But unconditionally, the record is Kim–Sarnak’s bound θ≤764\theta\leq\tfrac{7}{64}, based on the automorphy of symmetric fourth power LL-functions [28, Appendix 2].

This creates a power-saving gap between the best conditional and unconditional results in various arithmetic problems, for example, on the prime factors of quadratic polynomials [8, 37], the exponents of distribution of primes [32] and smooth numbers [39] in arithmetic progressions, and low-lying zeros of Dirichlet LL-functions [15]. Improvements to the dependency on θ\theta, which help narrow this gap, come from large sieve inequalities for the Fourier coefficients of exceptional Maass cusp forms (see [9, Theorems 5, 6, 7] and their optimizations in [14, 1, 32, 39]), which function as weak on-average substitutes for Selberg’s eigenvalue conjecture. However, in the key setting of fixed r,sr,s and sequences (an)(a_{n}) of length N≈r​sN\approx rs, no such savings were previously available.

Luckily, for many of the most important applications, we don’t need to handle 1.2 for completely arbitrary sequences, but only for those arising from variations of Linnik’s dispersion method [33, 18, 2, 3, 4]; these often have the rough form

(1.3) am=e⁡(m​α)andbn=∑h1,h2∼Hh1​ℓ1−h2​ℓ2=n1,a_{m}=e(m\alpha)\qquad\qquad\text{and}\qquad\qquad b_{n}=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}h_{1},h_{2}\sim H\\ h_{1}\ell_{1}-h_{2}\ell_{2}=n\end{subarray}}1,

for α∈ℝ/ℤ\alpha\in\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z} and ℓ1≍ℓ2≫H\ell_{1}\asymp\ell_{2}\gg H with (ℓ1,ℓ2)=1(\ell_{1},\ell_{2})=1. Our main results in this paper are new large sieve inequalities for such sequences, with Fourier transforms that obey strong concentration conditions. These are obtained by combining the framework of Deshouillers–Iwaniec with combinatorial ideas—specifically, with new estimates for bilinear sums of Kloosterman sums, stemming from a counting argument of Cilleruelo–Garaev [7]. The resulting improved bounds for 1.2 can then feed through to the strongest results on several well-studied arithmetic problems.

Figure 1 summarizes the results outlined above, which go from counting problems (on the top row), to exponential sums (middle row), to automorphic forms (bottom row), and then backwards. The transition between the first two rows is mostly elementary (using successive applications of Poisson summation, Cauchy–Schwarz, combinatorial decompositions, and/or sieve methods), while the transition between the last two rows uses the Kuznetsov trace formula [31, 9].

Before we dive into the large sieve inequalities, let us motivate our discussion with applications.

Theorem 1.

For infinitely many n∈ℤ+n\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}, the greatest prime factor of n2+1n^{2}+1 is larger than n1.3n^{1.3}.

This result makes progress on a longstanding problem, approximating the famous conjecture that there exist infinitely many primes of the form n2+1n^{2}+1. Back in 1967, Hooley [23] proved the same result with an exponent of 1.10011.1001, using the Weil bound for Kloosterman sums. In 1982, Deshouillers–Iwaniec [10] used their bounds on multilinear forms of Kloosterman sums [9] to improve this substantially, up to an exponent of 1.20241.2024. More recently, using Kim–Sarnak’s bound θ≤764\theta\leq\tfrac{7}{64} [28, Appendix 2], de la Bretèche and Drappeau [8] optimized the exponent to 1.21821.2182. Finally, Merikoski [37] proved a new bilinear estimate (still relying on the bounds of Deshouillers–Iwaniec [9]), and used Harman’s sieve to reach the exponent 1.2791.279; assuming Selberg’s eigenvalue conjecture, Merikoski also reached the conditional exponent 1.3121.312. With our new large sieve inequalities (Theorems 2 and 3), we can improve the arithmetic information due to both Merikoski [37] and de la Bretèche–Drappeau [8], leading to the unconditional result in Theorem 1. As in [37, 8], by adapting our proof, it should be possible to obtain similar results for other irreducible quadratic polynomials.

Additionally, we announce applications to the distribution of primes and smooth numbers in arithmetic progressions to large moduli. In [38], the author will show that the primes have exponent of distribution 5/8−ε5/8-\varepsilon using “triply-well-factorable” weights (λq)(\lambda_{q}) [35], in the sense that

∑q≤x5/8−ε(q,a)=1λq(π(x;q,a)−π⁡(x)φ⁡(q))≪ε,A,ax(log⁡x)A,\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}q\leq x^{5/8-\varepsilon}\\ (q,a)=1\end{subarray}}\lambda_{q}\left(\pi(x;q,a)-\frac{\pi(x)}{\varphi(q)}\right)\ll_{\varepsilon,A,a}\frac{x}{(\log x)^{A}},

where π⁡(x,q,a)\pi(x;q,a) denotes the number of primes up to xx which are congruent to aa mod qq. A similar result, with the same exponent of 5/8−ε5/8-\varepsilon, will be established for smooth numbers, using arbitrary 11-bounded weights (λq)(\lambda_{q}). These will improve results of Maynard [35] and Lichtman [32], respectively Drappeau [13] and the author [39]. Notably, our large sieve inequalities will suffice to completely eliminate the dependency on Selberg’s eigenvalue conjecture in these cases.

We also note that an extension of our large sieve inequalities to Maass forms with a general nebentypus should have consequences to counting smooth values of irreducible quadratic polynomials [8, 21, 22] (by improving de la Bretèche–Drappeau’s [8, Théorème 5.2]), and to enlarging the Fourier support in one-level density estimates for Dirichlet LL-functions [15].

1.1. The large sieve inequalities

We now turn to our main technical results. The sums of Kloosterman sums from 1.2 are related to the Fourier coefficients of GL2\mathrm{GL}_{2} automorphic forms of level q=r​sq=rs by the Kuznetsov trace formula [31, 9] for the congruence group Γ0​(q)\Gamma_{0}(q).

More precisely, the spectral side of the Kuznetsov formula contains three terms, corresponding to the contribution of holomorphic forms, Maass forms, and Eisenstein series. The exceptional Maass forms are eigenfunctions of the hyperbolic Laplacian on L2​(Γ0​(q)\ℍ)L^{2}(\Gamma_{0}(q)\backslash\mathbb{H}) with eigenvalues 0<λ<1/40<\lambda<1/4; this (conjecturally empty) exceptional spectrum typically produces losses of the form Xθ⁡(q)X^{\theta(q)}, where XX is a large parameter and θ⁡(q):=maxλ⁡max⁡(0,14−λ)\theta(q):=\max_{\lambda}\sqrt{\max(0,\tfrac{1}{4}-\lambda)}. The aforementioned large sieve inequalities for exceptional Maass forms can help alleviate this loss, by incorporating factors of XθX^{\theta}. Below we state a known result for general sequences (an)(a_{n}) (the values X∈{1,q/N}X\in\{1,q/N\} corresponding to [9, Theorems 2 and 5]), which we aim to improve; we detail our notation in Section 3.

Theorem A (Large sieve with general sequences [9]).

Let ε>0\varepsilon>0, X>0X>0, N≥1/2N\geq 1/2, and (an)n∼N(a_{n})_{n\sim N} be a complex sequence. Let q∈ℤ+q\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}, 𝔞\mathfrak{a} be a cusp of Γ0​(q)\Gamma_{0}(q) with μ⁡(𝔞)=q−1\mu(\mathfrak{a})=q^{-1}, and σ𝔞∈PSL2​(ℝ)\sigma_{\mathfrak{a}}\in\mathrm{PSL}_{2}(\mathbb{R}) be a scaling matrix for 𝔞\mathfrak{a}. Consider an orthonormal basis of Maass cusp forms for Γ0​(q)\Gamma_{0}(q), with eigenvalues λj\lambda_{j} and Fourier coefficients ρj​𝔞​(n)\rho_{j\mathfrak{a}}(n) around the cusp 𝔞\mathfrak{a} (via σ𝔞\sigma_{\mathfrak{a}}). Then with θj:=14−λj\theta_{j}:=\sqrt{\tfrac{1}{4}-\lambda_{j}}, one has

(1.4) ∑λj<1/4X2​θj|∑n∼Nanρj​𝔞(n)|2≪ε(qN)ε(1+Nq)∥an∥22,\sum_{\lambda_{j}<1/4}X^{2\theta_{j}}\left|\sum_{n\sim N}a_{n}\,\rho_{j\mathfrak{a}}(n)\right|^{2}\ll_{\varepsilon}(qN)^{\varepsilon}\left(1+\frac{N}{q}\right)\|a_{n}\|_{2}^{2},

for any

(1.5) X≪max⁡(1,qN,q2N3).X\ll\max\left(1,\frac{q}{N},\frac{q^{2}}{N^{3}}\right).
Remark.

As in [34, 39, 32], we use Deshouillers–Iwaniec’s normalization [9] for the Fourier coefficients ρj​𝔞​(n)\rho_{j\mathfrak{a}}(n) of Maass forms. In various other works [45, 14, 8, 37], ρj​𝔞​(n)\rho_{j\mathfrak{a}}(n) are rescaled by n−1/2n^{-1/2}.

Remark.

An equivalent (and more common [9, 14]) way to phrase results like Theorem A is that

∑λj<1/4X2​θj|∑n∼Nanρj​𝔞(n)|2≪ε(qN)ε(1+XX0)2​θ​(q)(1+Nq)∥an∥22,\sum_{\lambda_{j}<1/4}X^{2\theta_{j}}\left|\sum_{n\sim N}a_{n}\,\rho_{j\mathfrak{a}}(n)\right|^{2}\ll_{\varepsilon}(qN)^{\varepsilon}\left(1+\frac{X}{X_{0}}\right)^{2\theta(q)}\left(1+\frac{N}{q}\right)\|a_{n}\|_{2}^{2},

for any X>0X>0, and X0=X0​(N,q)X_{0}=X_{0}(N,q) given by the right-hand side of 1.5. We prefer to state our large sieve inequalities in terms of the maximal value of XX which does not produce any losses in the right-hand side, compared to the regular spectrum (i.e., X≪X0X\ll X_{0}). We note that in applications, one usually has q≪N≪q\sqrt{q}\ll N\ll q, and the best choice in 1.5 for this range is X≍q/NX\asymp q/N. But in the critical range N≍qN\asymp q, Theorem A is as good as the large sieve inequalities for the full spectrum [9, Theorem 2], since the limitation X≪1X\ll 1 forestalls any savings in the θ\theta-aspect.

When some averaging over levels q∼Qq\sim Q is available, 𝔞=∞\mathfrak{a}=\infty, and (an)(a_{n}), σ∞\sigma_{\infty} are independent of qq, Deshouillers–Iwaniec [9, Theorem 6] improved the admissible range to X≪max⁡(1,(Q/N)2)X\ll\max(1,(Q/N)^{2}); Lichtman [32] recently refined this to X≪max⁡(1,min⁡((Q/N)32/7,Q2/N))X\ll\max(1,\min((Q/N)^{32/7},Q^{2}/N)), by making θ\theta-dependencies explicit in [9, §8.2]. We note that these results are still limited at X≪1X\ll 1 when N≍QN\asymp Q.

Although it seems difficult to improve Theorem A in general (see Section 2.1), one can hope to do better for special sequences (an)(a_{n}); for instance, the last term in 1.5 can be improved if the sequence (an)(a_{n}) is sparse. In this paper, we consider the “dual” setting when (an)(a_{n}) is sparse in frequency space, i.e., when the Fourier transform a^​(ξ):=∑nan​e​(−n​ξ)\widehat{a}(\xi):=\sum_{n}a_{n}\,e(-n\xi) is concentrated on a subset of ℝ/ℤ\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}. We give a general result of this sort in Theorem 13, which also depends on rational approximations to the support of a^\widehat{a}. Below we state the two main cases of interest, corresponding to the sequences in 1.3 (we also incorporate a scalar aa in the Fourier coefficients, but on a first read one should take a=1a=1).

Theorem 2 (Large sieve with exponential phases).

Let ε,X>0\varepsilon,X>0, N≥1/2N\geq 1/2, α∈ℝ/ℤ\alpha\in\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}, and q,a∈ℤ+q,a\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}. Then with the notation of Theorem A and the choice of scaling matrix in 3.9, the bound

(1.6) ∑λj<1/4X2​θj|∑n∼Ne(nα)ρj​𝔞(an)|2≪ε(qaN)ε(1+a​Nq)N\sum_{\lambda_{j}<1/4}X^{2\theta_{j}}\left|\sum_{n\sim N}e(n\alpha)\,\rho_{j\mathfrak{a}}(an)\right|^{2}\ll_{\varepsilon}(qaN)^{\varepsilon}\left(1+\frac{aN}{q}\right)N

holds for all

(1.7) X≪max⁡(N,qa)mint∈ℤ+⁡(t+N​‖t​α‖).X\ll\frac{\max\left(N,\frac{q}{a}\right)}{\min_{t\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}}\left(t+N\|t\alpha\|\right)}.

In particular, this implies the range X≪max⁡(N,qa​N)X\ll\max(\sqrt{N},\tfrac{q}{a\sqrt{N}}), uniformly in α\alpha and σ𝔞\sigma_{\mathfrak{a}}. The same result holds if e⁡(n​α)e(n\alpha) is multiplied by Φ⁡(n/N)\Phi(n/N), for any smooth function Φ:(0,4)→ℂ\Phi:(0,4)\to\mathbb{C} with Φ(j)≪j1\Phi^{(j)}\ll_{j}1.

Here, ‖α‖\|\alpha\| denotes the distance from α\alpha to 00 inside ℝ/ℤ\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}; the fact that the worst (“minor-arc”) range covered by 1.7 is X≪max⁡(N,qa​N)X\ll\max(\sqrt{N},\tfrac{q}{a\sqrt{N}}) follows from a pigeonhole argument. The best range, X≪max⁡(N,qa)X\ll\max(N,\tfrac{q}{a}), is achieved when α\alpha is O⁡(N−1)O(N^{-1}) away from a rational number with bounded denominator. In particular, Theorem 2 obtains significant savings in the θ\theta-aspect in the critical case N≍qN\asymp q, for an individual level qq, which was previously impossible to the best of our knowledge.

Remark.

As detailed in Section 3.2, altering the scaling matrix σ𝔞\sigma_{\mathfrak{a}} in bounds like 1.6 is equivalent to altering the phase α\alpha; the canonical choice in 3.9 leads to several simplifications in practice.

For the second sequences mentioned in 1.3, we state a bound which also incorporates exponential phases e⁡(hi​αi)e(h_{i}\alpha_{i}). The reader should keep in mind the case of parameter sizes N≍H​LN\asymp HL, H≍LH\asymp L, and αi=0\alpha_{i}=0, when the XX-factor saved below can be as large as max⁡(N,qa​N)\max(\sqrt{N},\tfrac{q}{a\sqrt{N}}).

Some instances of the dispersion method [15, 14, 1] use coefficients roughly of the shape

Remark.

For simplicity, we state and prove our results in the setting of arbitrary bases of classical Maass forms, following the original work of Deshouillers–Iwaniec [9]. However, our work should admit two independent extensions, which are relevant for some applications. The first is handling Maass forms with a nontrivial nebentypus, following Drappeau [14]; this leads to bounds for sums like 1.2 with cc restricted to an arithmetic progression. The second is considering Hecke–Maass forms which are exceptional with respect to the Ramanujan–Petersson conjecture at finite places, the non-Archimedean analogue of Selberg’s conjecture; this should improve the dependency on the scalar aa when a​N>qaN>q. One could either follow Assing–Blomer–Li [1] to ‘factor out’ aa from ρj​𝔞​(a​n)\rho_{j\mathfrak{a}}(an) (and apply Kim–Sarnak’s bound [28] at places dividing aa before using our large sieve inequalities), or treat the exceptional forms at places dividing aa similarly to the Archimedean case, to match the regular-spectrum bound whenever a​XaX is at most a function of qq and NN (this option should work better when aa is well-factorable).

2. Informal overview

Let us summarize the key ideas behind our work, ignoring a handful of technical details such as smooth weights, GCD constraints, or keeping track of xo⁡(1)x^{o(1)} factors.

2.1. Large sieve with general sequences

Let q∈ℤ+q\in\mathbb{Z}_{+} and consider the simplified version

(2.1) ∑λj<1/4X2​θj​|∑n∼Nan​ρj​∞​(n)|2≲(1+Nq)​‖an‖22\sum_{\lambda_{j}<1/4}X^{2\theta_{j}}\left|\sum_{n\sim N}a_{n}\,\rho_{j\infty}(n)\right|^{2}\lesssim\left(1+\frac{N}{q}\right)\|a_{n}\|_{2}^{2}

of the large sieve inequality from Theorem A, for 𝔞=∞\mathfrak{a}=\infty, ignoring (q​N)o⁡(1)(qN)^{o(1)} factors. Here (an)(a_{n}) are arbitrary complex coefficients, and the reader may pretend that |an|≈1|a_{n}|\approx 1 for each nn, so that ‖an‖22≈N\|a_{n}\|_{2}^{2}\approx N. Such an inequality follows from [9, Theorem 2] when X=1X=1, but we need larger values of XX to temper the contribution of exceptional eigenvalues. The Kuznetsov trace formula [31] in Proposition E, combined with large sieve inequalities for the regular spectrum [9, Theorem 2], essentially reduces the problem to bounding (a smoothed variant of) the sum

(2.2) ∑c∼N​Xc≡0​(mod ​q)1c​∑m∼Nam¯​∑n∼Nan​S​(m,n,c)\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}c\sim NX\\ c\equiv 0\ (\textnormal{mod }q)\end{subarray}}\frac{1}{c}\sum_{m\sim N}\overline{a_{m}}\sum_{n\sim N}a_{n}\,S(m,n;c)

by the same amount as in the right-hand side of 2.1—see Corollary I for a formal statement in this direction. The left-hand side vanishes for X<q/(2​N)X<q/(2N), so we immediately obtain 2.1 for X≪q/NX\ll q/N, which is the content of [9, Theorem 5]. Alternatively, we can plug in the pointwise Weil bound for S⁡(m,n,c)S(m,n;c) and apply Cauchy–Schwarz, to obtain an upper bound of roughly

(2.3) N​Xq​1N​X​N​‖an‖22​N​X=N3/2​X1/2q​‖an‖22.\frac{NX}{q}\frac{1}{NX}N\|a_{n}\|_{2}^{2}\sqrt{NX}=\frac{N^{3/2}X^{1/2}}{q}\|a_{n}\|_{2}^{2}.

This is acceptable in 2.1 provided that X≤q2/N3X\leq q^{2}/N^{3}, which completes the range from Theorem A.

Improving the range X≤max⁡(1,q/N,q2/N3)X\leq\max(1,q/N,q^{2}/N^{3}) turns out to be quite difficult. Indeed, it is not clear how to exploit the averaging over cc without the Kuznetsov formula, so any savings are more likely to come from bounding bilinear forms of Kloosterman sums ∑m∼Nam​∑n∼Nbn​S​(m,n,c)\sum_{m\sim N}a_{m}\sum_{n\sim N}b_{n}\,S(m,n;c); this is a notoriously hard problem for general sequences (am),(bn)(a_{m}),(b_{n}) [29, 30, 27, 47]. For example, an extension of the work of Kowalski–Michel–Sawin [29] to general moduli should improve Theorem A in the critical range q≈N2q\approx N^{2}, but even then the final numerical savings would be relatively small.

The other critical case encountered in applications is q≈Nq\approx N, where Theorem A gives no non-trivial savings in the θ\theta-aspect (i.e., X≪1X\ll 1), and where such savings should in fact be impossible for general sequences (an)(a_{n}). Indeed, we expect |ρj​(n)||\rho_{j}(n)| to typically be of size ≈q−1/2\approx q^{-1/2}, so by picking an=q​ρ1​(n)¯a_{n}=q\,\overline{\rho_{1}(n)}, the left-hand side of 2.1 is at least X2​θ​(q)​N2X^{2\theta(q)}N^{2}, while the right-hand side is (1+Nq)​q​N(1+\frac{N}{q})qN; this limits the most optimistic savings for general sequences at X=(1+qN)1/(2​θ​(q))X=(1+\frac{q}{N})^{1/(2\theta(q))}.

The key idea in our work is to make use of the special structure of the sequences (an)(a_{n}) which show up in variations of the dispersion method [33]. Often, such sequences have sparse Fourier transforms, and using Fourier analysis on the corresponding exponential sums leads to a combinatorial problem.

2.2. Exponential phases and a counting problem

Let us focus on the case an=e⁡(n​α)a_{n}=e(n\alpha), for some α∈[0,1)\alpha\in[0,1). Expanding the Kloosterman sums from 2.2 and Fourier-completing in m,nm,n leads to a variant of the identity

(2.4) ∑m∼Ne⁡(−m​α)​∑n∼Ne⁡(n​α)​S​(m,n,c)≈N2​∑|x−c​α|≤c/N|y+c​α|≤c/Ne⁡(N⁡(x+y)c)​𝟙x​y≡1​(mod ​c).\sum_{m\sim N}e(-m\alpha)\sum_{n\sim N}e(n\alpha)\,S(m,n;c)\approx N^{2}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}|x-c\alpha|\leq c/N\\ |y+c\alpha|\leq c/N\end{subarray}}e\left(\frac{N(x+y)}{c}\right)\mathbbm{1}_{xy\equiv 1\ (\textnormal{mod }c)}.

Taking absolute values and ignoring the outer averaging over cc, we are left with the task of bounding

(2.5) ∑|x−c​α|≤X|y+c​α|≤X𝟙x​y≡1​(mod ​c),\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}|x-c\alpha|\leq X\\ |y+c\alpha|\leq X\end{subarray}}\mathbbm{1}_{xy\equiv 1\ (\textnormal{mod }c)},

for c∼N​Xc\sim NX, which is just a count of points on a modular hyperbola in short intervals (as considered in [7]). When α=0\alpha=0, one can directly use the divisor bound to write

∑|x|,|y|≤X𝟙x​y≡1​(mod ​c)=∑|z|≤X2c∑|x|,|y|≤X𝟙x​y=c​z+1≲X2c+1,\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}|x|,|y|\leq X\end{subarray}}\mathbbm{1}_{xy\equiv 1\ (\textnormal{mod }c)}=\sum_{|z|\leq\frac{X^{2}}{c}}\,\sum_{|x|,|y|\leq X}\mathbbm{1}_{xy=cz+1}\lesssim\frac{X^{2}}{c}+1,

up to a factor of Xo⁡(1)X^{o(1)}, which leads to a variant of

∑m,n∼NS⁡(m,n,c)≲c+N2=N​X+N2.\sum_{m,n\sim N}S(m,n;c)\lesssim c+N^{2}=NX+N^{2}.

(This type of bound was also observed by Shparlinski and Zhang [43].) Overall, we roughly obtain

(2.6) ∑c∼N​Xc≡0​(mod ​q)1c​∑m,n∼NS⁡(m,n,c)≲N​X+N2q,\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}c\sim NX\\ c\equiv 0\ (\textnormal{mod }q)\end{subarray}}\frac{1}{c}\sum_{m,n\sim N}S(m,n;c)\lesssim\frac{NX+N^{2}}{q},

which is at most (1+Nq)​N(1+\frac{N}{q})N, as required in 2.1, provided that

X≤max⁡(N,q).X\leq\max(N,q).

This gives the best-case range from 1.7 (when a=1a=1). The analogue of this argument for other values of α∈ℝ/ℤ\alpha\in\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z} depends on the quality of the best rational approximations to α\alpha, due to a rescaling trick of Cilleruelo–Garaev [7]. For an arbitrary value of α\alpha, a pigeonhole argument (Dirichlet approximation) leads to a bound of the shape

(2.7) ∑c∼N​Xc≡0​(mod ​q)1c​∑m∼Ne⁡(−m​α)​∑n∼Ne⁡(n​α)​S​(m,n,c)≲N3/2​X+N2q,\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}c\sim NX\\ c\equiv 0\ (\textnormal{mod }q)\end{subarray}}\frac{1}{c}\sum_{m\sim N}e(-m\alpha)\sum_{n\sim N}e(n\alpha)\,S(m,n;c)\lesssim\frac{N^{3/2}X+N^{2}}{q},

and ultimately to the range X≤max⁡(N,q/N)X\leq\max(\sqrt{N},q/\sqrt{N}), which is the worst (and average) case in 1.7 when a=1a=1. Incorporating a scalar aa inside ρj​∞​(a​n)\rho_{j\infty}(an) is not too difficult, since a similar argument handles the analogous bilinear sums of S⁡(a​m,a​n,c)S(am,an;c), up to a loss of gcd⁡(a,c)\gcd(a,c).

Remark.

A consequence of not leveraging the exponential phases in the right-hand side of 2.4 is that the same argument extends to sums over |m|,|n|≤N|m|,|n|\leq N. In particular, the term m=n=0m=n=0 already gives a contribution of about c≍N​Xc\asymp NX, which produces a term of N​X/qNX/q in 2.6 with a linear growth in XX (as opposed to the square-root growth from 2.3, coming from the Weil bound).

2.3. Sequences with frequency concentration

It will probably not come as a surprise that one can extend the preceeding discussion by Fourier-expanding other sequences (an)(a_{n}), given a strong-enough concentration condition for their Fourier transforms, but there are some subtleties in how to do this optimally. If an=μˇ​(n)=∫ℝ/ℤe⁡(n​α)​𝑑μ​(α)a_{n}=\check{\mu}(n)=\int_{\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}}e(n\alpha)\,d\mu(\alpha) for all n∼Nn\sim N and some bounded-variation complex measure μ\mu, then there are at least two ways to proceed—depending on whether the integral over α\alpha is kept inside or outside of the square.

Indeed, by applying Cauchy–Schwarz in α\alpha and our Theorem 2 for exponential phases as a black-box, one can directly obtain a bound like

(2.8) ∑λj<1/4X2​θj​|∑n∼Nan​ρj​𝔞​(n)|2≲(1+Nq)​N​|μ|​(ℝ/ℤ)2,\sum_{\lambda_{j}<1/4}X^{2\theta_{j}}\left|\sum_{n\sim N}a_{n}\,\rho_{j\mathfrak{a}}(n)\right|^{2}\lesssim\left(1+\frac{N}{q}\right)N|\mu|(\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z})^{2},

for all X≤max⁡(N,q/N)X\leq\max(\sqrt{N},q/\sqrt{N}) (and this range can be slightly improved given more information about the support of μ\mu near rational numbers of small denominators). Unfortunately, this replaces the norm ‖an‖2\|a_{n}\|_{2} from Theorem A with N​|μ|​(ℝ/ℤ)\sqrt{N}|\mu|(\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}), which produces a significant loss unless μ\mu is very highly concentrated—and it is difficult to make up for this loss through gains of X2​θX^{2\theta}.

The alternative approach is to expand the square in the left-hand side of 2.8, pass to a sum of Kloosterman sums as in 2.2 by Kuznetsov, and only then Fourier-expand (two instances of) the sequence (an)(a_{n}). Using similar combinatorial ideas as for 2.7, we can then essentially bound

(2.9) ∑c∼N​Xc≡0​(mod ​q)1c​∑m∼Ne⁡(m​α)​∑n∼Ne⁡(n​β)​S​(m,n,c)≲N5/3​X+N2q,\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}c\sim NX\\ c\equiv 0\ (\textnormal{mod }q)\end{subarray}}\frac{1}{c}\sum_{m\sim N}e(m\alpha)\sum_{n\sim N}e(n\beta)\,S(m,n;c)\lesssim\frac{N^{5/3}X+N^{2}}{q},

for arbitrary values of α,β∈ℝ/ℤ\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}. With no further information about the support of μ\mu, this ultimately gives a bound like

∑λj<1/4X2​θj​|∑n∼Nan​ρj​𝔞​(n)|2≲(1+Nq)​‖an‖22+N5/3​X+N2q​|μ|​(ℝ/ℤ)2,\sum_{\lambda_{j}<1/4}X^{2\theta_{j}}\left|\sum_{n\sim N}a_{n}\,\rho_{j\mathfrak{a}}(n)\right|^{2}\lesssim\left(1+\frac{N}{q}\right)\|a_{n}\|_{2}^{2}+\frac{N^{5/3}X+N^{2}}{q}|\mu|(\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z})^{2},

which is acceptable in 2.1, in particular, whenever X<N1/3X<N^{1/3} and N​|μ|​(ℝ/ℤ)≤q/N​‖an‖2\sqrt{N}|\mu|(\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z})\leq\sqrt{q/N}\|a_{n}\|_{2}. Compared to the first approach, this generally gains less in the XX-aspect, but it relaxes the concentration condition on μ\mu if N<qN<q. This second approach turns out to be better for our applications; the resulting large sieve inequality is Theorem 13, which particularizes to Theorems 2 and 3.

What is perhaps more surprising, though, is that strong-enough frequency concentration (i.e., N​|μ|​(ℝ/ℤ)2≤q/N​‖an‖2\sqrt{N}|\mu|(\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z})^{2}\leq\sqrt{q/N}\|a_{n}\|_{2}) arises in applications, beyond the case of exponential sequences. A key observation is that the aforementioned dispersion coefficients

(2.10) an=∑h1,h2∼Hh1​ℓ1−h2​ℓ2=n1,a_{n}=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}h_{1},h_{2}\sim H\\ h_{1}\ell_{1}-h_{2}\ell_{2}=n\end{subarray}}1,

with ℓ1≍ℓ2≍L\ell_{1}\asymp\ell_{2}\asymp L, come from a convolution of two “arithmetic progressions” 𝟙n≡0​(mod ​ℓi)​𝟙n∼H​ℓi\mathbbm{1}_{n\equiv 0\ (\textnormal{mod }\ell_{i})}\mathbbm{1}_{n\sim H\ell_{i}}. The Fourier transform of each of these two sequences has ℓi\ell_{i} periodic peaks of height HH and width (H​ℓi)−1(H\ell_{i})^{-1}, supported around multiples of 1/ℓi1/\ell_{i}. When (ℓ1,ℓ2)=1(\ell_{1},\ell_{2})=1, multiplying these two Fourier transforms results in cancellation everywhere away from a small number (≤1+LH\leq 1+\frac{L}{H}) of rational points (and thus, in frequency concentration on a set of size 1H​L+1H2\frac{1}{HL}+\frac{1}{H^{2}}); see Lemma 11.

2.4. Multilinear forms of Kloosterman sums

Consider once again the sums 1.2, in the ranges

M,N≤r​s,X:=s​r​CM​N≥1,M,N\leq rs,\qquad\qquad X:=\frac{s\sqrt{r}C}{\sqrt{MN}}\geq 1,

which are relevant for most applications. An additional use of the Kuznetsov formula, for the level q=r​sq=rs and the cusps ∞,1/s\infty,1/s (with suitable scaling matrices), gives a variant of the bound

∑m∼Mam​∑n∼Nbn​∑(c,r)=1g⁡(cC)​S​(m​r¯,±n,s​c)\displaystyle\sum_{m\sim M}a_{m}\sum_{n\sim N}b_{n}\sum_{(c,r)=1}g\left(\frac{c}{C}\right)S(m\overline{r},\pm n;sc)
≲s​r​C​∑λj<1/4X2​θj​|∑m∼Mam​ρj​∞​(m)|​|∑n∼Nbn​ρj​ 1/s​(n)|+…\displaystyle\lesssim s\sqrt{r}C\sum_{\lambda_{j}<1/4}X^{2\theta_{j}}\left|\sum_{m\sim M}a_{m}\,\rho_{j\infty}(m)\right|\left|\sum_{n\sim N}b_{n}\,\rho_{j\,1/s}(n)\right|\ +\ \ldots

Here we omitted the contribution of the regular Maass forms, Eisenstein series and holomorphic forms (which will not be dominant). A priori, this arrangement introduces a factor of X2​θ​(q)X^{2\theta(q)} in our bounds, recalling that θ⁡(q)=maxλj​(q)<1/4⁡θj​(q)\theta(q)=\max_{\lambda_{j}(q)<1/4}\theta_{j}(q) (if the maximum is nonempty, and θ⁡(q)=0\theta(q)=0 otherwise). However, the value of XX in this loss can be decreased through the large sieve inequalities for exceptional Maass forms. Indeed, after splitting X=X0​X1​X2X=X_{0}\sqrt{X_{1}X_{2}}, taking out a factor of only (1+X0)2​θ​(q)(1+X_{0})^{2\theta(q)}, and applying Cauchy–Schwarz, we reach

s​r​C​(1+X0)2​θ​(q)​(∑λj<1/4X12​θj​|∑m∼Mam​ρj​∞​(m)|2)1/2​(∑λj<1/4X22​θj​|∑n∼Nbn​ρj​ 1/s​(n)|2)1/2.s\sqrt{r}C\,(1+X_{0})^{2\theta(q)}\left(\sum_{\lambda_{j}<1/4}X_{1}^{2\theta_{j}}\left|\sum_{m\sim M}a_{m}\,\rho_{j\infty}(m)\right|^{2}\right)^{1/2}\left(\sum_{\lambda_{j}<1/4}X_{2}^{2\theta_{j}}\left|\sum_{n\sim N}b_{n}\,\rho_{j\,1/s}(n)\right|^{2}\right)^{1/2}.

Above, we can choose X1X_{1} and X2X_{2} as the maximal values that can be fully incorporated in large sieve inequalities like 2.1 without producing losses in the right-hand side, for the specific sequences (am)(a_{m}) and (bn)(b_{n}). In this case, we roughly obtain a final bound of

s​r​C​(1+s​r​CM​N​X1​X2)2​θ​(q)​‖am‖2​‖bn‖2.s\sqrt{r}C\left(1+\frac{s\sqrt{r}C}{\sqrt{MNX_{1}X_{2}}}\right)^{2\theta(q)}\|a_{m}\|_{2}\,\|b_{n}\|_{2}.

For example, if am=e⁡(m​αr,s)a_{m}=e(m\alpha_{r,s}) for some αr,s∈ℝ/ℤ\alpha_{r,s}\in\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}, then we may take X1=max⁡(N,q/N)X_{1}=\max(\sqrt{N},q/\sqrt{N}) by Theorem 2, which ultimately saves a factor of Nθ/2N^{\theta/2}. Similarly, if (bn)(b_{n}) are of the form in 2.10, where H≍L≍NH\asymp L\asymp\sqrt{N}, then by Theorem 3 we may also take X2=max⁡(N,q/N)X_{2}=\max(\sqrt{N},q/\sqrt{N}).

If some averaging over r∼R,s∼Sr\sim R,s\sim S is available and the sequence (am)(a_{m}) does not depend on r,sr,s, then larger values of X1X_{1} are available due to Deshouillers–Iwaniec [9, Theorems 6, 7]. In this setting, if am=e⁡(m​ω)a_{m}=e(m\omega) for a fixed ω∈ℝ/ℤ\omega\in\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}, one can combine the essentially-optimal value X1=Q2/NX_{1}=Q^{2}/N (see Theorem J below) with our savings in the X2X_{2}-aspect. Following [9, Theorem 12], similar estimates can be deduced for multilinear forms of incomplete Kloosterman sums, simply by Fourier-completing them and appealing to the estimates for complete sums; see our Corollary 18. Such bounds feed directly into the dispersion method and its applications, as we shall see in Section 6.

2.5. Layout of paper

In Section 3, we cover notation and preliminary results, including several key lemmas from the spectral theory of automorphic forms. Section 4 only contains elementary arguments, from counting points on modular hyperbolas in Lemma 8 (following Cilleruelo–Garaev [7]), to the bilinear Kloosterman bounds in Proposition 10 (which may be of independent interest to the reader). In Section 5.1, we combine these combinatorial inputs with the Deshouillers–Iwaniec setup [9] to prove a general large sieve inequality in Theorem 13, which can be viewed as our main technical result; we then deduce Theorems 2 and 3 from it. Section 5.3 contains the corollaries of these large sieve inequalities: various bounds for multilinear forms of Kloosterman sums, with improved dependencies on the θ\theta parameter. Finally, in Section 6 we will use these bounds to prove Theorem 1, building on the work of Merikoski [37] and de la Bretèche–Drappeau [8].

3. Notation and preliminaries

3.1. Standard analytic notation

We write ℤ,ℚ,ℝ,ℂ,ℍ\mathbb{Z},\mathbb{Q},\mathbb{R},\mathbb{C},\mathbb{H} for the sets of integers, rational numbers, real numbers, complex numbers, respectively complex numbers with positive imaginary part. We may scale these sets by constants, and may add the subscript ++ to restrict to positive numbers; so for example 2​ℤ+2\mathbb{Z}_{+} denotes the set of even positive integers, while i​ℝi\mathbb{R} is the imaginary line. For α∈ℝ\alpha\in\mathbb{R} (or ℝ/ℤ\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}), we denote e⁡(α):=exp⁡(2​π​i​α)e(\alpha):=\exp(2\pi i\alpha), and set ‖α‖:=minn∈ℤ⁡|α−n|\|\alpha\|:=\min_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}|\alpha-n|, which induces a metric on ℝ/ℤ\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}. We write ℤ/c​ℤ\mathbb{Z}/c\mathbb{Z} for the ring of residue classes modulo a positive integer cc, (ℤ/c​ℤ)×(\mathbb{Z}/c\mathbb{Z})^{\times} for its multiplicative group of units, and x¯\overline{x} for the inverse of x∈(ℤ/c​ℤ)×x\in(\mathbb{Z}/c\mathbb{Z})^{\times}. We may use the latter notation inside congruences, with x≡y​z¯​(mod ​c)x\equiv y\overline{z}\ (\textnormal{mod }c) meaning that x​z≡y⁡(mod ​c)xz\equiv y\ (\textnormal{mod }c) (for gcd⁡(z,c)=1\gcd(z,c)=1). We may also use the notation (a,b)(a,b) for gcd⁡(a,b)\gcd(a,b), and [a,b][a,b] for lcm⁡(a,b)\mathrm{lcm}(a,b), when it is clear from context to not interpret these as pairs or intervals. We write 𝟙S\mathbbm{1}_{S} for the indicator function of a set SS (or for the truth value of a statement SS), n∼Nn\sim N for the statement that N<n≤2​NN<n\leq 2N (so, e.g., 𝟙n∼N=𝟙n≤2​N−𝟙n≤N\mathbbm{1}_{n\sim N}=\mathbbm{1}_{n\leq 2N}-\mathbbm{1}_{n\leq N}), and interpret sums like ∑n∼N\sum_{n\sim N}, ∑n≡0​(mod ​q)\sum_{n\equiv 0\ (\textnormal{mod }q)}, or ∑d|n\sum_{d\mid n} with the implied restrictions that n,d∈ℤ+n,d\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}. For n∈ℤ+n\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}, we define the divisor-counting function by τ⁡(n):=∑d|n1\tau(n):=\sum_{d\mid n}1, and Euler’s totient function by φ⁡(n):=∑m=1n𝟙(m,n)=1\varphi(n):=\sum_{m=1}^{n}\mathbbm{1}_{(m,n)=1}. We say that a complex sequence (an)(a_{n}) is divisor-bounded iff |an|≪τ​(n)O⁡(1)|a_{n}|\ll\tau(n)^{O(1)}. We also write P+​(n)P^{+}(n) and P−​(n)P^{-}(n) for the largest and smallest prime factors of a positive integer nn, and recall that nn is called yy-smooth iff P+​(n)≤yP^{+}(n)\leq y.

We use the standard asymptotic notation f≪gf\ll g, f≍gf\asymp g, f=O⁡(g)f=O(g), f=ox→∞​(g)f=o_{x\to\infty}(g) from analytic number theory, and indicate that the implicit constants depend on some parameter ε\varepsilon through subscripts (e.g., f≪εgf\ll_{\varepsilon}g, f=Oε​(g)f=O_{\varepsilon}(g)). In particular, one should read bounds like f⁡(x)≪xo⁡(1)f(x)\ll x^{o(1)} as ∀ε>0,f(x)≪εxε\forall\varepsilon>0,\,f(x)\ll_{\varepsilon}x^{\varepsilon}. Given ℓ∈ℤ+\ell\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}, we write f(ℓ)f^{(\ell)} for the ℓ\ellth derivative of a function f:ℝ→ℂf:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{C}, and f(0)=ff^{(0)}=f. For q∈[1,∞]q\in[1,\infty], we denote by ‖f‖Lq\|f\|_{L^{q}} the LqL^{q}-norm of a function f:ℝ→ℂf:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{C} (or f:ℝ/ℤ→ℂf:\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{C}), and by ‖a‖q\|a\|_{q} (or ‖an‖q\|a_{n}\|_{q}) the ℓq\ell^{q} norm of a sequence (an)(a_{n}).

We require multiple notations for the Fourier transforms of L1L^{1} functions f,Φ:ℝ→ℂf,\Phi:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{C}, φ:ℝ/ℤ→ℂ\varphi:\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{C}, and a:ℤ→ℂa:\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{C} (the latter could be, e.g., a finite sequence (an)n∼N(a_{n})_{n\sim N} extended with zeroes elsewhere). These are given by

(3.1) f:ℝ→ℂ↝f^:ℂ→ℂ,\displaystyle f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{C}\qquad\leadsto\qquad\,\,\widehat{f}:\mathbb{C}\to\mathbb{C}, f^​(ξ):=∫ℝf⁡(t)​e​(−ξ​t)​dt,\displaystyle\widehat{f}(\xi):=\int_{\mathbb{R}}f(t)\,e(-\xi t)\ dt,
Φ:ℝ→ℂ↝Φˇ:ℂ→ℂ,\displaystyle\Phi:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{C}\qquad\leadsto\qquad\,\check{\Phi}:\mathbb{C}\to\mathbb{C}, Φˇ​(t):=∫ℝΦ⁡(ξ)​e​(ξ​t)​dξ,\displaystyle\check{\Phi}(t):=\int_{\mathbb{R}}\Phi(\xi)\,e(\xi t)\ d\xi,
a:ℤ→ℂ↝a^:ℝ/ℤ→ℂ,\displaystyle a:\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{C}\quad\ \ \,\,\leadsto\ \ \,\,\widehat{a}:\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{C}, a^(α):=∑n∈ℤane(−nα),\displaystyle\widehat{a}(\alpha):=\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}a_{n}\,e(-n\alpha),\qquad
φ:ℝ/ℤ→ℂ↝φˇ:ℤ→ℂ,\displaystyle\varphi:\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{C}\qquad\leadsto\qquad\ \check{\varphi}:\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{C}, φˇ​(n):=∫ℝ/ℤφ⁡(α)​e​(n​α)​dα.\displaystyle\check{\varphi}(n):=\int_{\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}}\varphi(\alpha)\,e(n\alpha)\,d\alpha.

Note that the first two and the last two of these transforms are inverse operations under suitable conditions; in particular, if Φ\Phi is Schwarz, aa is L1L^{1}, and φ\varphi is smooth (so φˇ​(n)\check{\varphi}(n) decays rapidly as |n|→∞|n|\to\infty), one has

(3.2) Φ^ˇ|ℝ=Φˇ^|ℝ=Φ,a^ˇ=a,φˇ^=φ.\check{\widehat{\Phi}}\Big|_{\mathbb{R}}=\widehat{\check{\Phi}}\Big|_{\mathbb{R}}=\Phi,\qquad\qquad\check{\widehat{a}}=a,\qquad\qquad\widehat{\check{\varphi}}=\varphi.

We also denote the Fourier transform of a bounded-variation complex Borel measure μ\mu on ℝ/ℤ\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z} by μˇ​(n):=∫ℝ/ℤe⁡(n​α)​𝑑μ​(α)\check{\mu}(n):=\int_{\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}}e(n\alpha)\,d\mu(\alpha). For instance, one has λˇ​(n)=𝟙n=0\check{\lambda}(n)=\mathbbm{1}_{n=0} for the Lebesgue measure λ\lambda, and δˇA​(n)=∑α∈Ae⁡(n​α)\check{\delta}_{A}(n)=\sum_{\alpha\in A}e(n\alpha) for the Dirac delta measure on a finite set A⊂ℝ/ℤA\subset\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}. Moreover, if d​μ=φ​d​λd\mu=\varphi\,d\lambda for some L1L^{1} function φ:ℝ/ℤ→ℂ\varphi:\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{C}, then μˇ=φˇ\check{\mu}=\check{\varphi}. Finally, with our notation, the Parseval–Plancherel identity reads ‖an‖22=‖a^‖L22\|a_{n}\|_{2}^{2}=\|\widehat{a}\|_{L^{2}}^{2} (and ‖f‖L2=‖f^‖L2\|f\|_{L^{2}}=\|\widehat{f}\|_{L^{2}}), while Poisson summation states that for any Schwarz function ff,

(3.3) ∑n∈ℤf⁡(n)=∑n∈ℤf^​(n)=∑n∈ℤfˇ​(n).\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}f(n)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}\widehat{f}(n)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}\check{f}(n).

In practice it will be useful to truncate the Poisson summation formula; we combine this with a smooth dyadic partition of unity and a separation of variables, in the following lemma.

We also highlight the non-standard Notation 5, pertaining to rational approximations. Further analytic notation specific to each section is described therein (see, e.g., 12, 20 and 23). For the rest of this section, we recount the main concepts relevant to bounding sums of Kloosterman sums via the Kuznetsov trace formula, mostly to clarify our notation (in particular, to point out small changes to the notation in [9]), and to explicitate a few useful lemmas.

3.2. Cusps, automorphic forms, Kloosterman sums

Recall that PSL2​(ℝ):=SL2​(ℝ)/{±1}\mathrm{PSL}_{2}(\mathbb{R}):=\mathrm{SL}_{2}(\mathbb{R})/\{\pm 1\} acts naturally on ℂ∪{∞}\mathbb{C}\cup\{\infty\} by (abcd)​z:=a​z+bc​z+d\left(\begin{smallmatrix}a&b\\ c&d\end{smallmatrix}\right)z:=\frac{az+b}{cz+d}. For q∈ℤ+q\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}, we denote by Γ0​(q)\Gamma_{0}(q) the modular subgroup of level qq, consisting of those matrices (abcd)∈PSL2​(ℤ)\left(\begin{smallmatrix}a&b\\ c&d\end{smallmatrix}\right)\in\mathrm{PSL}_{2}(\mathbb{Z}) with c≡0​(mod ​q)c\equiv 0\ (\textnormal{mod }q). A number 𝔞∈ℂ∪{∞}\mathfrak{a}\in\mathbb{C}\cup\{\infty\} is called a cusp of Γ0​(q)\Gamma_{0}(q) iff it is the unique fixed point of some σ∈Γ0​(q)\sigma\in\Gamma_{0}(q); we write Γ𝔞:={σ∈Γ0​(q):σ​𝔞=𝔞}\Gamma_{\mathfrak{a}}:=\{\sigma\in\Gamma_{0}(q):\sigma\mathfrak{a}=\mathfrak{a}\} for the stabilizer of 𝔞\mathfrak{a} inside Γ0​(q)\Gamma_{0}(q). Two cusps are equivalent iff they lie in the same orbit of Γ0​(q)\Gamma_{0}(q); the corresponding stabilizers are then conjugate inside Γ0​(q)\Gamma_{0}(q). By [9, Lemma 2.3], the fractions

(3.5) {uw:u,w∈ℤ+,(u,w)=1,w∣q,u≤gcd(w,qw)}\left\{\frac{u}{w}\ :\ u,w\in\mathbb{Z}_{+},\ (u,w)=1,\ w\mid q,\ u\leq\gcd\left(w,\frac{q}{w}\right)\right\}

form a maximal set of inequivalent cusps of Γ0​(q)\Gamma_{0}(q). Following [9, (1.1)], given a cusp 𝔞\mathfrak{a} of Γ0​(q)\Gamma_{0}(q) and its equivalent representative u/wu/w from 3.5, we denote

(3.6) μ⁡(𝔞):=gcd⁡(w,qw)q,\mu(\mathfrak{a}):=\frac{\gcd\left(w,\frac{q}{w}\right)}{q},

(Like most of our notation involving cusps, this implicitly depends on the level qq as well.) In particular, the cusp at ∞\infty of Γ0​(q)\Gamma_{0}(q) is equivalent to the fraction 1/q1/q, so we have μ⁡(∞)=q−1\mu(\infty)=q^{-1}. More generally, we have μ⁡(1/s)=q−1\mu(1/s)=q^{-1} whenever q=r​sq=rs with gcd⁡(r,s)=1\gcd(r,s)=1, and it is these cusps which account for most applications to sums of Kloosterman sums; thus for simplicity, we restrict all of our main results to cusps with μ⁡(𝔞)=q−1\mu(\mathfrak{a})=q^{-1}. Following [9, (1.2)], a scaling matrix σ𝔞\sigma_{\mathfrak{a}} for a cusp 𝔞\mathfrak{a} is an element of PSL2​(ℝ)\mathrm{PSL}_{2}(\mathbb{R}) such that

(3.7) σ𝔞​∞=𝔞andσ𝔞−1​Γ𝔞​σ𝔞=Γ∞={(1n01):n∈ℤ}.\sigma_{\mathfrak{a}}\infty=\mathfrak{a}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\sigma_{\mathfrak{a}}^{-1}\Gamma_{\mathfrak{a}}\sigma_{\mathfrak{a}}=\Gamma_{\infty}=\left\{\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&n\\ 0&1\end{smallmatrix}\right):n\in\mathbb{Z}\right\}.

Scaling matrices will allow us to expand Γ𝔞\Gamma_{\mathfrak{a}}-invariant functions f:ℍ→ℂf:\mathbb{H}\to\mathbb{C} as Fourier series around the cusp 𝔞\mathfrak{a}, via the change of coordinates z←σ𝔞​zz\leftarrow\sigma_{\mathfrak{a}}z (note that if ff is Γ𝔞\Gamma_{\mathfrak{a}}-invariant, then z↦f⁡(σ𝔞​z)z\mapsto f(\sigma_{\mathfrak{a}}z) is Γ∞\Gamma_{\infty}-invariant). For a given cusp 𝔞\mathfrak{a}, the choice of σ𝔞\sigma_{\mathfrak{a}} can only vary by simple changes of coordinates

(3.8) σ~𝔞=σ𝔞​(1α01),\widetilde{\sigma}_{\mathfrak{a}}=\sigma_{\mathfrak{a}}\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&\alpha\\ 0&1\end{smallmatrix}\right),

for α∈ℝ\alpha\in\mathbb{R} (which result in multiplying the Fourier coefficients by exponential phases e⁡(n​α)e(n\alpha)). When μ⁡(𝔞)=q−1\mu(\mathfrak{a})=q^{-1}, we must have 𝔞=τ⁡(1/s)\mathfrak{a}=\tau(1/s) for some τ∈Γ0​(q)\tau\in\Gamma_{0}(q) and r​s=qrs=q with (r,s)=1(r,s)=1; in this case, inspired by Watt [46, p. 195], we will use the canonical choice of scaling matrix

(3.9) σ𝔞=τ⋅(r−s¯/rs​rr¯​r),\sigma_{\mathfrak{a}}=\tau\cdot\left(\begin{smallmatrix}\sqrt{r}&-\overline{s}/\sqrt{r}\\ s\sqrt{r}&\overline{r}\sqrt{r}\end{smallmatrix}\right),

where r¯,s¯\overline{r},\overline{s} are integers such that r​r¯+s​s¯=1r\overline{r}+s\overline{s}=1 (for definiteness, let us say we pick s¯≥0\overline{s}\geq 0 to be minimal). This is different from the choice in [9, (2.3)], and leads to the simplification of certain extraneous exponential phases. For the cusp 𝔞=∞=(10−q1)​(1/q)\mathfrak{a}=\infty=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&0\\ -q&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)(1/q), 3.9 reduces back to the identity matrix.

We refer the reader to the aforementioned work of Deshouillers–Iwaniec [9] for a brief introduction to the classical spectral theory of GL2\mathrm{GL}_{2} automorphic forms, to [25, 24, 26] for a deeper dive into this topic, to [14, 45, 15, 8, 32, 39] for follow-up works and optimizations, and to [6] for the modern viewpoint of automorphic representations. For our purposes, an automorphic form of level qq and integer weight k≥0k\geq 0 will be a smooth function f:ℍ→ℂf:\mathbb{H}\to\mathbb{C} satisfying the transformation law

f⁡(σ​z)=j​(σ,z)k​f​(z)∀σ∈Γ0​(q),wherej⁡((abcd),z):=c​z+d.f(\sigma z)=j(\sigma,z)^{k}f(z)\qquad\forall\sigma\in\Gamma_{0}(q),\qquad\text{where}\qquad j\left(\left(\begin{smallmatrix}a&b\\ c&d\end{smallmatrix}\right),z\right):=cz+d.

as well as moderate (at-most-polynomial) growth conditions near every cusp. We say that ff is square-integrable iff ⟨f,f⟩k<∞\left\langle f,f\right\rangle_{k}<\infty, where ⟨f,g⟩k:=∬Γ0​(q)\ℍf⁡(x+i​y)​g⁡(x+i​y)¯​yk−2​𝑑x​𝑑y\left\langle f,g\right\rangle_{k}:=\iint_{\Gamma_{0}(q)\backslash\mathbb{H}}f(x+iy)\,\overline{g(x+iy)}\,y^{k-2}\,dx\,dy is the Petersson inner product. We denote by L2​(Γ0​(q)\ℍ,k)L^{2}(\Gamma_{0}(q)\backslash\mathbb{H},k) the space of square-integrable automorphic forms of level qq and weight kk; when we drop the dependency on kk, it should be understood that k=0k=0. Finally, we call ff a cusp form iff it is square-integrable and vanishes at all cusps.

Kloosterman sums show up in the Fourier coefficients of Poincaré series, which are useful in detecting the Fourier coefficients of other automorphic forms via inner products (see [9, (1.8), (1.18)]). In fact, by Fourier expanding a Poincaré series corresponding to a cusp 𝔞\mathfrak{a} around another cusp 𝔟\mathfrak{b}, one is led to a more general family of Kloosterman-type sums, depending on both 𝔞\mathfrak{a} and 𝔟\mathfrak{b}.

More specifically (following [9, (1.3)], [14, §4.1.1], [24]), given two cusps 𝔞,𝔟\mathfrak{a},\mathfrak{b} of Γ0​(q)\Gamma_{0}(q), we first let

𝒞𝔞​𝔟:={c∈ℝ+:∃a,b,d∈ℝ,(abcd)∈σ𝔞−1Γ0(q)σ𝔟}.\mathcal{C}_{\mathfrak{a}\mathfrak{b}}:=\left\{c\in\mathbb{R}_{+}:\exists\,a,b,d\in\mathbb{R},\left(\begin{smallmatrix}a&b\\ c&d\end{smallmatrix}\right)\in\sigma_{\mathfrak{a}}^{-1}\Gamma_{0}(q)\,\sigma_{\mathfrak{b}}\right\}.

Here σ𝔞\sigma_{\mathfrak{a}} and σ𝔟\sigma_{\mathfrak{b}} are arbitrary scaling matrices for 𝔞\mathfrak{a} and 𝔟\mathfrak{b}, but the set 𝒞𝔞​𝔟\mathcal{C}_{\mathfrak{a}\mathfrak{b}} actually depends only on 𝔞\mathfrak{a} and 𝔟\mathfrak{b} (since multiplication by matrices (1α01)\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&\alpha\\ 0&1\end{smallmatrix}\right) does not affect the bottom-left entry). Then we let

𝒟𝔞​𝔟(c):={d~∈ℝ/cℤ:∃a,b∈ℝ,d∈d~,(abcd)∈σ𝔞−1Γ0(q)σ𝔟},\mathcal{D}_{\mathfrak{a}\mathfrak{b}}(c):=\left\{\widetilde{d}\in\mathbb{R}/c\mathbb{Z}:\exists\,a,b\in\mathbb{R},\,d\in\widetilde{d},\left(\begin{smallmatrix}a&b\\ c&d\end{smallmatrix}\right)\in\sigma_{\mathfrak{a}}^{-1}\Gamma_{0}(q)\,\sigma_{\mathfrak{b}}\right\},

for any c∈ℝ+c\in\mathbb{R}_{+} (although this is only nonempty when c∈𝒞𝔞​𝔟c\in\mathcal{C}_{\mathfrak{a}\mathfrak{b}}). By this definition, the set 𝒟𝔞​𝔟​(c)\mathcal{D}_{\mathfrak{a}\mathfrak{b}}(c) is finite, does not depend on σ𝔞\sigma_{\mathfrak{a}}, and only depends on σ𝔟\sigma_{\mathfrak{b}} up to translations. It turns out that a given d~∈𝒟𝔞​𝔟​(c)\widetilde{d}\in\mathcal{D}_{\mathfrak{a}\mathfrak{b}}(c) uniquely determines the value of a~∈ℝ/c​ℤ\widetilde{a}\in\mathbb{R}/c\mathbb{Z} such that (abcd)∈σ𝔞−1​Γ0​(q)​σ𝔟\left(\begin{smallmatrix}a&b\\ c&d\end{smallmatrix}\right)\in\sigma_{\mathfrak{a}}^{-1}\Gamma_{0}(q)\,\sigma_{\mathfrak{b}} for some a∈a~a\in\widetilde{a}, d∈d~d\in\widetilde{d} (see [9, p. 239]). Symmetrically, this a~\widetilde{a} does not depend on σ𝔟\sigma_{\mathfrak{b}}, and only depends on σ𝔞\sigma_{\mathfrak{a}} up to translations. Thus given c∈ℝ+c\in\mathbb{R}_{+} and m,n∈ℤm,n\in\mathbb{Z}, it makes sense to define

(3.10) S𝔞​𝔟​(m,n,c):=∑d~∈𝒟𝔞​𝔟​(c)e⁡(m​a~+n​d~c),S_{\mathfrak{a}\mathfrak{b}}(m,n;c):=\sum_{\widetilde{d}\in\mathcal{D}_{\mathfrak{a}\mathfrak{b}}(c)}e\left(\frac{m\widetilde{a}+n\widetilde{d}}{c}\right),

where a~\widetilde{a} and d~\widetilde{d} are corresponding values mod cc; note that this vanishes unless c∈𝒞𝔞​𝔟c\in\mathcal{C}_{\mathfrak{a}\mathfrak{b}}. Since varying the choices of σ𝔞\sigma_{\mathfrak{a}} and σ𝔟\sigma_{\mathfrak{b}} has the effect of uniformly translating a~\widetilde{a}, respectively d~\widetilde{d}, it follows that S𝔞​𝔟​(m,n,c)S_{\mathfrak{a}\mathfrak{b}}(m,n;c) only depends on σ𝔞,σ𝔟\sigma_{\mathfrak{a}},\sigma_{\mathfrak{b}} up to multiplication by exponential phases e⁡(m​α)e(m\alpha), e⁡(n​β)e(n\beta). In fact, the same holds true when varying 𝔞\mathfrak{a} and 𝔟\mathfrak{b} in equivalence classes of cusps [9, p. 239]. We also note the symmetries

(3.11) S𝔞​𝔟​(m,−n,c)=S𝔞​𝔟​(−m,n,c)¯,S𝔞​𝔟​(m,n,c)=S𝔟​𝔞​(n,m,c)¯,S_{\mathfrak{a}\mathfrak{b}}(m,-n;c)=\overline{S_{\mathfrak{a}\mathfrak{b}}(-m,n;c)},\qquad\qquad S_{\mathfrak{a}\mathfrak{b}}(m,n;c)=\overline{S_{\mathfrak{b}\mathfrak{a}}(n,m;c)},

the second one following from the fact that

(abcd)∈σ𝔞−1Γ0(q)σ𝔟⇔(−dbc−a)=−(abcd)−1∈σ𝔟−1Γ0(q)σ𝔞.\left(\begin{smallmatrix}a&b\\ c&d\end{smallmatrix}\right)\in\sigma_{\mathfrak{a}}^{-1}\Gamma_{0}(q)\,\sigma_{\mathfrak{b}}\qquad\iff\qquad\left(\begin{smallmatrix}-d&b\\ c&-a\end{smallmatrix}\right)=-\left(\begin{smallmatrix}a&b\\ c&d\end{smallmatrix}\right)^{-1}\in\sigma_{\mathfrak{b}}^{-1}\Gamma_{0}(q)\,\sigma_{\mathfrak{a}}.

Let us now relate these sums to the classical Kloosterman sums from 1.1.

Lemma B (Explicit Kloosterman sums [46]).

Let q=r​sq=rs with r,s∈ℤ+r,s\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}, gcd⁡(r,s)=1\gcd(r,s)=1. Then for any c∈ℝ+c\in\mathbb{R}_{+} and m,n∈ℤm,n\in\mathbb{Z}, with the choice of scaling matrices from 3.9, one has

(3.12) S∞​ 1/s​(m,n,s​r​c)=𝟙c∈ℤ+,(c,r)=1​S​(m​r¯,n,s​c).S_{\infty\,1/s}\left(m,n;s\sqrt{r}c\right)=\mathbbm{1}_{c\in\mathbb{Z}_{+},\,(c,r)=1}\,S(m\overline{r},n;sc).

Moreover, let 𝔞\mathfrak{a} be any cusp of Γ0​(q)\Gamma_{0}(q) with μ⁡(𝔞)=q−1\mu(\mathfrak{a})=q^{-1}, and σ𝔞\sigma_{\mathfrak{a}} be as in 3.9. Then one has

(3.13) S𝔞​𝔞​(m,n,c)=𝟙c∈q​ℤ+​S​(m,n,c).S_{\mathfrak{a}\mathfrak{a}}(m,n;c)=\mathbbm{1}_{c\in q\mathbb{Z}_{+}}\,S(m,n;c).

Varying the choice of scaling matrix as in 3.8 would result in an additional factor of e⁡((n−m)​α)e((n-m)\alpha).

Proof.

These identities are precisely [46, (3.5) and (3.4)], at least when 𝔞=1/s\mathfrak{a}=1/s for some r​s=qrs=q, with (r,s)=1(r,s)=1. For a general cusp with μ⁡(𝔞)=q−1\mu(\mathfrak{a})=q^{-1}, we have 𝔞=τ⁡(1/s)\mathfrak{a}=\tau(1/s) for some τ∈Γ0​(q)\tau\in\Gamma_{0}(q), but the presence of τ\tau in the scaling matrix from 3.9 does not affect the set σ𝔞−1​Γ0​(q)​σ𝔞\sigma_{\mathfrak{a}}^{-1}\Gamma_{0}(q)\,\sigma_{\mathfrak{a}}, nor the generalized Kloosterman sum S𝔞​𝔞​(m,n,c)S_{\mathfrak{a}\mathfrak{a}}(m,n;c). For explicit computations of this type, see [9, §2]. ∎

3.3. The Kuznetsov formula and exceptional eigenvalues

We now recognize some important classes of GL2\mathrm{GL}_{2} automorphic forms of level qq:

  • (1).

    Classical modular forms, which are holomorphic with removable singularities at all cusps, and can only have even weights k∈2​ℤ+k\in 2\mathbb{Z}_{+} (except for the zero form). A holomorphic cusp form ff additionally vanishes at all cusps; such forms have Fourier expansions

    (3.14) j​(σ𝔞,z)−k​f​(σ𝔞​z)=∑n=1∞ψ𝔞​(n)​e​(n​z)j(\sigma_{\mathfrak{a}},z)^{-k}f(\sigma_{\mathfrak{a}}z)=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\psi_{\mathfrak{a}}(n)\,e(nz)

    around each cusp 𝔞\mathfrak{a} of Γ0​(q)\Gamma_{0}(q) (see [9, (1.7)]). We mention that the space of holomorphic cusp forms of weight kk is finite-dimensional, and denote its dimension by hk=hk​(q)h_{k}=h_{k}(q).

  • (2).

    Maass forms (of weight 00), which are invariant under the action of Γ0​(q)\Gamma_{0}(q), and are eigenfunctions of the hyperbolic Laplacian Δ=−y2(∂x2+∂y2)\Delta=-y^{2}\left(\partial_{x}^{2}+\partial_{y}^{2}\right). These include:

    • (a).

      Maass cusp forms, which additionally vanish at all cusps and are square-integrable. These (plus the constant functions) correspond to the discrete spectrum of the hyperbolic Laplacian on L2​(Γ0​(q)\ℍ)L^{2}\left(\Gamma_{0}(q)\backslash\mathbb{H}\right), consisting of eigenvalues 0=λ0<λ1≤λ2≤λ3≤…0=\lambda_{0}<\lambda_{1}\leq\lambda_{2}\leq\lambda_{3}\leq\ldots with no limit point. Around a given cusp 𝔞\mathfrak{a}, Maass cusp forms have Fourier expansions (see [9, (1.15)])

      (3.15) u⁡(σ𝔞​z)=y1/2​∑n≠0ρ𝔞​(n)​Ki​κ​(2​π​|n|​y)​e​(m​x),u(\sigma_{\mathfrak{a}}z)=y^{1/2}\sum_{n\neq 0}\rho_{\mathfrak{a}}(n)K_{i\kappa}(2\pi|n|y)\,e(mx),

      where z=x+i​yz=x+iy and KK is the Whittaker function normalized as in [9, p. 264].

    • (b).

      Eisenstein series, explicitly defined by E𝔞​(z,s):=∑τ∈Γ𝔞\Γ0​(q)Ims​(σ𝔞−1​τ​z)E_{\mathfrak{a}}(z;s):=\sum_{\tau\in\Gamma_{\mathfrak{a}}\backslash\Gamma_{0}(q)}\mathrm{Im}^{s}\left(\sigma_{\mathfrak{a}}^{-1}\tau z\right) for Re​s>1\mathrm{Re}\,s>1, and meromorphically continued to s∈ℂs\in\mathbb{C}. Although not square-integrable themselves, “incomplete” versions of Eisenstein series with s=12+i​rs=\frac{1}{2}+ir (and r∈ℝr\in\mathbb{R}) can be used to describe the orthogonal complement in L2​(Γ0​(q)\ℍ)L^{2}\left(\Gamma_{0}(q)\backslash\mathbb{H}\right) of the space of Maass cusp forms, corresponding to the continuous spectrum of the hyperbolic Laplacian. Sharing similarities with both Maass cusp forms and Poincaré series, the Eisenstein series E𝔞E_{\mathfrak{a}} have Fourier expansions [9, (1.17)] around any cusp 𝔟\mathfrak{b}, involving the Whittaker function and the Kloosterman-resembling coefficients (for n∈ℤn\in\mathbb{Z}, n≠0n\neq 0)

      (3.16) φ𝔞​𝔟​(n,s):=∑c∈𝒞𝔞​𝔟c−2​s​∑d~∈𝒟𝔞​𝔟​(c)e⁡(n​d~c).\varphi_{\mathfrak{a}\mathfrak{b}}(n;s):=\sum_{c\in\mathcal{C}_{\mathfrak{a}\mathfrak{b}}}c^{-2s}\sum_{\widetilde{d}\in\mathcal{D}_{\mathfrak{a}\mathfrak{b}}(c)}e\left(\frac{n\widetilde{d}}{c}\right).

We are particularly interested in the exceptional Maass cusp forms, which have eigenvalues λj∈(0,1/4)\lambda_{j}\in(0,1/4); there can only be finitely many such forms of each level qq, and Selberg conjectured [41] that there are none. With implicit dependencies on qq, we denote

(3.17) κj2:=λj−14andθj:=i​κj,\kappa_{j}^{2}:=\lambda_{j}-\frac{1}{4}\qquad\qquad\text{and}\qquad\qquad\theta_{j}:=i\kappa_{j},

where κj\kappa_{j} is chosen such that i​κj>0i\kappa_{j}>0 or κj≥0\kappa_{j}\geq 0; thus exceptional forms correspond to imaginary values of κj\kappa_{j} and positive values of θj\theta_{j}. Letting

θ⁡(q):=max⁡(0,14−λ1​(q))={θ1​(q),θ1​(q)>00,otherwise.,θmax:=supq≥1θ⁡(q),\theta(q):=\sqrt{\max\left(0,\tfrac{1}{4}-\lambda_{1}(q)\right)}=\begin{cases}\theta_{1}(q),&\theta_{1}(q)>0\\ 0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases},\qquad\qquad\theta_{\max}:=\sup_{q\geq 1}\,\theta(q),

Selberg’s eigenvalue conjecture asserts that θmax=0\theta_{\max}=0, and the best result towards it is due to Kim–Sarnak [28, Appendix 2]. This deep unconditional result requires the theory of GLn\mathrm{GL}_{n} automorphic representations [6], but it is a very useful black-box input to spectral methods, where various bounds have exponential dependencies on θ\theta.

Theorem C (Kim–Sarnak’s eigenvalue bound [28]).

One has θmax≤764\theta_{\max}\leq\tfrac{7}{64}.

Based on earlier work of Kuznetsov [31], Deshouillers–Iwaniec [9] developed a trace formula relating weighted sums over cc of the generalized Kloosterman sums from 3.10 to (sums of products of) the Fourier coefficients of holomorphic cusp forms, Maass cusp forms, and Eisenstein series, around any two cusps 𝔞,𝔟\mathfrak{a},\mathfrak{b} of Γ0​(q)\Gamma_{0}(q). Roughly speaking, this follows by summing two applications of Parseval’s identity for the aforementioned Poincaré series: one in the space of holomorphic cusp forms (summing over all weights k∈2​ℤ+k\in 2\mathbb{Z}_{+}), and one in the space L2​(Γ0​(q)/ℍ)L^{2}(\Gamma_{0}(q)/\penalty\mathbb{H}) of square-integrable automorphic forms of weight 00, via the spectral decomposition of the hyperbolic Laplacian (leading to the terms from Maass cusp forms and Eisenstein series).

One can arrange the resulting Kuznetsov trace formula so that the Kloosterman sums in the left-hand side are weighted by an arbitrary compactly-supported smooth function φ\varphi; in the right-hand side, the Fourier coefficients of automorphic forms are consequently weighted by Bessel transforms of φ\varphi, defined for r∈ℝ∖{0}r\in\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\} by

(3.18) ℬ~φ​(r)\displaystyle\widetilde{\mathcal{B}}_{\varphi}(r) :=∫0∞Jr​(y)​φ​(y)​d​yy,\displaystyle:=\int_{0}^{\infty}J_{r}(y)\,\varphi(y)\frac{dy}{y},
ℬ^φ​(r)\displaystyle\widehat{\mathcal{B}}_{\varphi}(r) :=πsinh⁡(π​r)​∫0∞J2​i​r​(x)−J−2​i​r​(x)2​i​φ​(x)​d​xx,\displaystyle:=\frac{\pi}{\sinh(\pi r)}\int_{0}^{\infty}\frac{J_{2ir}(x)-J_{-2ir}(x)}{2i}\varphi(x)\frac{dx}{x},
ℬˇφ​(r)\displaystyle\check{\mathcal{B}}_{\varphi}(r) :=4π​cosh⁡(π​r)​∫0∞K2​i​r​(x)​φ​(x)​d​xx,\displaystyle:=\frac{4}{\pi}\cosh(\pi r)\int_{0}^{\infty}K_{2ir}(x)\,\varphi(x)\frac{dx}{x},

where Ki​tK_{it} is the aforementioned Whittaker function, and the Bessel functions JℓJ_{\ell}, Ji​tJ_{it} are defined as in [9, p. 264–265] (above we slightly departed from the notation in [9, 14], to avoid confusion with Fourier transforms). All we will need to know about these transforms are the following bounds.

Lemma D (Bessel transform bounds [9]).

Let Y>0Y>0 and φ:ℝ→ℂ\varphi:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{C} be a smooth function with compact support in y≍Yy\asymp Y, satisfying φ(j)(y)≪jY−j\varphi^{(j)}(y)\ll_{j}Y^{-j} for j≥0j\geq 0. Then one has

Moreover, if φ\varphi is nonnegative with ∫φ⁡(y)​𝑑y≫Y\int\varphi(y)\,dy\gg Y, and Y<cY<c for some constant c≪1c\ll 1 (depending on the implied constants so far), then one has

(3.23) ℬ^φ​(κ)\displaystyle\widehat{\mathcal{B}}_{\varphi}(\kappa) ≍Y−2​i​κ, for ​ 0<i​κ<12.\displaystyle\asymp Y^{-2i\kappa},\qquad\qquad\,\text{ for }\ 0<i\kappa<\frac{1}{2}.
Proof.

The bounds in 3.19, 3.20 and 3.21 constitute [9, Lemma 7.1] (note that φ\varphi satisfies the requirements in [9, (1.43) and (1.44)] for (Y,1)(Y,1) in place of (X,Y)(X,Y)). Similarly, 3.22 and the lower bound in 3.23 are [9, (8.2) and (8.3), following from (8.1)], using an appropriate choice of the constants η1,η2\eta_{1},\eta_{2}. The upper bound in 3.23 also follows from [9, (8.1)], but is in fact already covered by 3.19 (using r=−i​κr=-i\kappa and the fact that ℬ^φ\widehat{\mathcal{B}}_{\varphi} is even). ∎

Finally, let us state the Kuznetsov trace formula, following the notation of Deshouillers–Iwaniec [9].

Remark.

Upon inspecting the Maass contribution 3.26 in light of the bounds 3.19 and 3.23, the losses due to the exceptional spectrum are apparent. Indeed, if φ⁡(y)\varphi(y) is supported in y≍Y≍m​nCy\asymp Y\asymp\frac{\sqrt{mn}}{C} for some C>0C>0 (indicating the size of cc), then the Bessel transforms bounds for exceptional eigenvalues are (a priori) worse by a factor of

max⁡(1,Y−2​θ​(q))≍(1+Cm​n)2​θ​(q),\max\left(1,Y^{-2\theta(q)}\right)\asymp\left(1+\frac{C}{\sqrt{mn}}\right)^{2\theta(q)},

compared to the regular (non-exceptional) spectrum.

3.4. Bounds for Fourier coefficients

If one is interested in a particular holomorphic or Maass cusp form (ideally, a Hecke eigenform), then various bounds for its Fourier coefficients follow from the theory of automorphic representations and their LL-functions [9, 40, 28, 6, 19, 20]. Here we are interested in bounding averages over bases of automorphic forms, resembling those that show up in 3.26, 3.25 and 3.27; naturally, these would be useful in combination with the Kuznetsov formula.

Remarkably, such bounds are often derived using the Kuznetsov formula once again (with different parameters, including the support range of the smooth function φ\varphi), together with various bounds for sums of Kloosterman sums, such as the Weil bound below.

Lemma F (Weil–Ramanujan bound).

For any c∈ℤ+c\in\mathbb{Z}_{+} and m,n∈ℤm,n\in\mathbb{Z}, one has

S⁡(m,n,c)≪τ⁡(c)​(m,n,c)1/2​c1/2.S(m,n;c)\ll\tau(c)\,(m,n,c)^{1/2}c^{1/2}.

Also, for m=0m=0, one has |S⁡(0,n,c)|≤(n,c)|S(0,n;c)|\leq(n,c).

Proof.

See [26, Corollary 11.12] for the first bound; the second bound, concerning Ramanujan sums, is classical and follows by Möbius inversion. ∎

The first results that we mention keep the index nn of the Fourier coefficients fixed, while varying the automorphic form.

is bounded up to a constant depending on ε\varepsilon by

K2+(q​n​K)ε​(q,n)1/2​μ​(𝔞)​n1/2.K^{2}+(qnK)^{\varepsilon}\,(q,n)^{1/2}\,\mu(\mathfrak{a})\,n^{1/2}.

These bounds roughly follow by combining Lemma F with trace formulas like Proposition E, for m=nm=n and suitable choices of φ\varphi. See for example [44, Lemmas 2.7 and 2.9] with q0=1q_{0}=1 and X=X0X=X_{0}, noting the different normalizations of the Fourier coefficients. ∎

Finally, for the results with averaging over the level qq, we will also need the following theorem of Deshouillers–Iwaniec [9].

Theorem J (Deshouillers–Iwaniec’s large sieve with level averaging [9]).

Let ε>0\varepsilon>0, X>0X>0, N,Q≥1/2N,Q\geq 1/2, and ω∈ℝ/ℤ\omega\in\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}. Then with the notation of Proposition E, one has

(3.34) ∑q∼Q∑λj​(q)<1/4X2​θj​(q)|∑n∼Ne(nω)ρj​∞q(n)|2≪ε(QN)ε(Q+N)N,\sum_{q\sim Q}\sum_{\lambda_{j}(q)<1/4}X^{2\theta_{j}(q)}\left|\sum_{n\sim N}e(n\omega)\,\rho_{j\infty_{q}}(n)\right|^{2}\ll_{\varepsilon}(QN)^{\varepsilon}\left(Q+N\right)N,

for any

(3.35) X≪max⁡(N,Q2N).X\ll\max\left(N,\frac{Q^{2}}{N}\right).
Proof.

This follows immediately from [9, Theorem 1.7] with X←X1/2X\leftarrow X^{1/2}. As noted in previous works [39, 3, 8], although [9, Theorem 7] was only stated for α=0\alpha=0, the same proof holds uniformly in α∈ℝ/ℤ\alpha\in\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}. ∎

4. Combinatorial bounds

In this section, we obtain bounds for bilinear sums of the form ∑mam​∑nbn​S​(m,n,c)\sum_{m}a_{m}\sum_{n}b_{n}\,S(m,n;c) (say, in the range c1/4≪N≪cc^{1/4}\ll N\ll c), saving over the Pólya–Vinogradov and Weil bounds if the Fourier transforms a^\widehat{a} and b^\widehat{b} are concentrated enough. Our computations here are elementary (not requiring the spectral theory of automorphic forms yet, nor any other prerequisites beyond Section 3.1), and use a combinatorial argument inspired by [7]; the latter was also used, e.g., in [27].

We highlight the following non-standard notation.

Notation 5 (Rational approximation).

Given M,N>0M,N>0, let TM,N:(ℝ/ℤ)2→ℝT_{M,N}:(\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z})^{2}\to\mathbb{R} denote the function

(4.1) TM,N​(α,β):=mint∈ℤ+⁡(t+M​‖α​t​‖+N‖​β​t‖)(abbreviating ​TN:=TN,N,TN​(α):=TN​(α,α)).\begin{gathered}T_{M,N}(\alpha,\beta):=\min_{t\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}}\left(t+M\|\alpha t\|+N\|\beta t\|\right)\\ (\text{abbreviating }T_{N}:=T_{N,N},\,T_{N}(\alpha):=T_{N}(\alpha,\alpha)).\end{gathered}

This measures how well α\alpha and β\beta can be simultaneously approximated by rational numbers with small denominators tt, in terms of the balancing parameters M,NM,N. The inverses of these parameters indicate the scales at which TM,N​(α,β)T_{M,N}(\alpha,\beta) has roughly constant size, due to the following lemma.

Lemma 6 (Basic properties of TM,NT_{M,N}).

Let M,N>0M,N>0 and α,β,γ,δ∈ℝ/ℤ\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\delta\in\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}. One has TN,M​(β,α)=TM,N​(α,β)=TM,N​(±α,±β)T_{N,M}(\beta,\alpha)=T_{M,N}(\alpha,\beta)=T_{M,N}(\pm\alpha,\pm\beta) and

(4.2) TN​(α,β±α)≍TN​(α,β).T_{N}(\alpha,\beta\pm\alpha)\asymp T_{N}(\alpha,\beta).

Moreover,

(4.3) TM,N​(α+γ,β)≤(1+M​‖γ‖)​TM,N​(α,β).T_{M,N}(\alpha+\gamma,\beta)\leq(1+M\|\gamma\|)\,T_{M,N}(\alpha,\beta).

In particular, if ‖γ‖≪M−1\|\gamma\|\ll M^{-1} and ‖δ‖≪N−1\|\delta\|\ll N^{-1}, then

(4.4) TM,N​(α+γ,β+δ)≍TM,N​(α,β).T_{M,N}\left(\alpha+\gamma,\beta+\delta\right)\asymp T_{M,N}(\alpha,\beta).
Proof.

The first equalities are obvious, and 4.2 follows from the triangle inequalities

‖(β±α)​t‖≤‖α​t‖+‖β​t‖,‖β​t‖≤‖α​t‖+‖(β±α)​t‖.\|(\beta\pm\alpha)t\|\leq\|\alpha t\|+\|\beta t\|,\qquad\qquad\|\beta t\|\leq\|\alpha t\|+\|(\beta\pm\alpha)t\|.

For 4.3, we note that

t+M​‖(α+γ)​t​‖+N‖​β​t‖\displaystyle t+M\|(\alpha+\gamma)t\|+N\|\beta t\| ≤t+M​‖γ​t​‖+M‖​α​t​‖+N‖​β​t‖\displaystyle\leq t+M\|\gamma t\|+M\|\alpha t\|+N\|\beta t\|
≤t⁡(1+M​‖γ‖)+M​‖α​t​‖+N‖​β​t‖\displaystyle\leq t(1+M\|\gamma\|)+M\|\alpha t\|+N\|\beta t\|
≤(1+M​‖γ‖)​(t+M​‖α​t​‖+N‖​β​t‖),\displaystyle\leq(1+M\|\gamma\|)\left(t+M\|\alpha t\|+N\|\beta t\|\right),

and take a minimum of both sides over t∈ℤ+t\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}. Finally, 4.4 follows immediately from 4.3. ∎

Lemma 7 (Dirichlet-style approximation).

Let α,β∈ℝ/ℤ\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}. Given any parameters A,B≫1A,B\gg 1, there exists a positive integer tt such that

t≪A​B,‖α​t‖≪1A,‖β​t‖≪1B.t\ll AB,\qquad\qquad\|\alpha t\|\ll\frac{1}{A},\qquad\qquad\|\beta t\|\ll\frac{1}{B}.

In particular, for N≥1/2N\geq 1/2, one has

(4.5) TN​(α,β)≪min⁡(N⁡(1+‖α−β‖​N),N2/3).T_{N}(\alpha,\beta)\ll\min\left(\sqrt{N(1+\|\alpha-\beta\|N)},N^{2/3}\right).
Proof.

Consider the sequence of points {(t​α,t​β)}t≤⌈A⌉​⌈B⌉+2\{(t\alpha,t\beta)\}_{t\leq\lceil A\rceil\lceil B\rceil+2} in (ℝ/ℤ)2(\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z})^{2}; by the pigeonhole principle, at least two of these must lie in a box of dimensions A−1×B−1A^{-1}\times B^{-1}, say (ti​α,ti​β)(t_{i}\alpha,t_{i}\beta) for i∈{1,2}i\in\{1,2\}. Then we can pick t:=|t1−t2|t:=|t_{1}-t_{2}| to establish the first claim.

Using A=B=N1/3A=B=N^{1/3}, we find that

TN​(α,β)≪N2/3,T_{N}(\alpha,\beta)\ll N^{2/3},

uniformly in α,β∈ℝ/ℤ\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}. Using A=N/(1+‖β‖​N)A=\sqrt{N/(1+\|\beta\|N)} and B=1B=1, we also have

TN​(α,β)≤mint∈ℤ+⁡(t+N⁡(‖α​t‖+‖β‖​t))\displaystyle T_{N}(\alpha,\beta)\leq\min_{t\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}}\left(t+N\left(\|\alpha t\|+\|\beta\|t\right)\right) ≪A+NA+N​‖β‖​A\displaystyle\ll A+\frac{N}{A}+N\|\beta\|A
≪N⁡(1+‖β‖​N),\displaystyle\ll\sqrt{N(1+\|\beta\|N)},

and thus

TN​(α,β)≪TN​(α,α−β)≪N⁡(1+‖α−β‖​N).T_{N}(\alpha,\beta)\ll T_{N}(\alpha,\alpha-\beta)\ll\sqrt{N(1+\|\alpha-\beta\|N)}.

This proves 4.5. ∎

Lemma 8 (Concentration of points on modular hyperbolas, following Cilleruelo–Garaev [7]).

Let c∈ℤ+c\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}, a,b,λ∈ℤ/c​ℤa,b,\lambda\in\mathbb{Z}/c\mathbb{Z}, 0<X,Y≪c0<X,Y\ll c, and I,J⊂ℝI,J\subset\mathbb{R} be intervals of lengths |I|=X|I|=X, |J|=Y|J|=Y. Then for any ε>0\varepsilon>0 and any (c​α,c​β)∈I×J(c\alpha,c\beta)\in I\times J, one has

(4.6) #{(x,y)∈(I∩ℤ)×(J∩ℤ):xy≡λ(mod c)}≪εcε(X​YcTcX,cY(α,β)+gcd(λ,c)),\#\left\{(x,y)\in(I\cap\mathbb{Z})\times(J\cap\mathbb{Z}):xy\equiv\lambda\ (\textnormal{mod }c)\right\}\ll_{\varepsilon}c^{\varepsilon}\left(\frac{XY}{c}\,T_{\frac{c}{X},\frac{c}{Y}}\left(\alpha,\beta\right)+\gcd(\lambda,c)\right),

with TM,N​(α,β)T_{M,N}(\alpha,\beta) as in Notation 5.

Remark.

Lemma 8 counts solutions to the congruence x​y≡λ⁡(mod ​c)xy\equiv\lambda\ (\textnormal{mod }c) in short intervals. On average over intervals of length X,Y≫cX,Y\gg\sqrt{c}, one should expect around X​Y/cXY/c solutions; 4.6 essentially recovers this average bound when α\alpha and β\beta can be simultaneously approximated by rational numbers with a bounded denominator.

Remark.

One can also interpret Lemma 8 in terms of sum-product phenomena over ℤ/c​ℤ\mathbb{Z}/c\mathbb{Z}. Indeed, the intervals a+[−X,X]a+[-X,X] and b+[−Y,Y]b+[-Y,Y] have many “additive collisions” of the form x1+y1≡x2+y2​(mod ​c)x_{1}+y_{1}\equiv x_{2}+y_{2}\ (\textnormal{mod }c) (with x1,x2∈a+[−X,X]x_{1},x_{2}\in a+[-X,X] and y1,y2∈b+[−Y,Y]y_{1},y_{2}\in b+[-Y,Y]), so they should have few “multiplicative collisions” of the form x1​y1≡λ≡x2​y2​(mod ​c)x_{1}y_{1}\equiv\lambda\equiv x_{2}y_{2}\ (\textnormal{mod }c).

Proof.

If I∩ℤ=∅I\cap\mathbb{Z}=\emptyset or J∩ℤ=∅J\cap\mathbb{Z}=\emptyset, the claim is trivial. So let a∈I∩ℤa\in I\cap\mathbb{Z} and b∈J∩ℤb\in J\cap\mathbb{Z}; by a change of variables, we have

#⁡{(x,y)∈I×J:x​y≡λ⁡(mod ​c)}≤#​S​(a,b),\#\{(x,y)\in I\times J:xy\equiv\lambda\ (\textnormal{mod }c)\}\leq\#S(a,b),

where

S⁡(a,b):={(x,y)∈([−X,X]∩ℤ)×([−Y,Y]∩ℤ):(x+a)​(y+b)≡λ⁡(mod ​c)}.S(a,b):=\{(x,y)\in([-X,X]\cap\mathbb{Z})\times([-Y,Y]\cap\mathbb{Z}):(x+a)(y+b)\equiv\lambda\ (\textnormal{mod }c)\}.

The key idea, borrowed from [7, Theorem 1] (and also used, for example, in [27, Lemma 5.3]), is to effectively reduce the size of aa and bb by appropriately scaling the congruence (x+a)​(y+b)≡λ⁡(mod ​c)(x+a)(y+b)\equiv\lambda\ (\textnormal{mod }c), and then to pass to an equation in the integers. Indeed, let t∈ℤ+t\in\mathbb{Z}_{+} be a scalar, and let a′,b′a^{\prime},b^{\prime} be the integers with minimal absolute values such that

(4.7) a​t≡a′​(mod ​c)andb​t≡b′​(mod ​c).at\equiv a^{\prime}\ (\textnormal{mod }c)\qquad\quad\text{and}\qquad\quad bt\equiv b^{\prime}\ (\textnormal{mod }c).

Then any given pair (x,y)∈S⁡(a,b)(x,y)\in S(a,b) also satisfies the scaled congruence

t(x+a)(y+b)≡tλ(mod c)⇔txy+b′x+a′y≡t(λ−ab)(mod c).t(x+a)(y+b)\equiv t\lambda\ (\textnormal{mod }c)\qquad\iff\qquad txy+b^{\prime}x+a^{\prime}y\equiv t(\lambda-ab)\ (\textnormal{mod }c).

Denoting by r∈{0,1,…,c−1}r\in\{0,1,\ldots,c-1\} the residue of t​(λ−a​b)​(mod ​c)t(\lambda-ab)\ (\textnormal{mod }c), and

z=z⁡(x,y):=t​x​y+b′​x+a′​y−rc,z=z(x,y):=\frac{txy+b^{\prime}x+a^{\prime}y-r}{c},

it follows that (x,y,z)(x,y,z) is an integer solution to the equation

txy+b′x+a′y=cz+r⇔(tx+a′)(ty+b′)=t(cz+r)+a′b′.txy+b^{\prime}x+a^{\prime}y=cz+r\qquad\Leftrightarrow\qquad(tx+a^{\prime})(ty+b^{\prime})=t(cz+r)+a^{\prime}b^{\prime}.

Note that

z\displaystyle z ≪t​X​Y+|b′|​X+|a′|​Y+cc\displaystyle\ll\frac{tXY+|b^{\prime}|X+|a^{\prime}|Y+c}{c}
≪tc​X​Y+‖b​tc‖​X+‖a​tc‖​Y+1=:Z⁡(t).\displaystyle\ll\frac{t}{c}XY+\left\|\frac{bt}{c}\right\|X+\left\|\frac{at}{c}\right\|Y+1=:Z(t).

Now let n⁡(z):=t⁡(c​z+r)+a′​b′n(z):=t(cz+r)+a^{\prime}b^{\prime}. The number of pairs (x,y)∈S⁡(a,b)(x,y)\in S(a,b) with n⁡(z)≠0n(z)\neq 0 is at most

∑z≪Z⁡(t)n⁡(z)≠0∑x,y∈ℤ(t​x+a′)​(t​y+b′)=n⁡(z)(x+a)​(y+b)≡λ⁡(mod ​c)1≪ε(ct)εZ(t),\displaystyle\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}z\ll Z(t)\\ n(z)\neq 0\end{subarray}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}x,y\in\mathbb{Z}\\ (tx+a^{\prime})(ty+b^{\prime})=n(z)\\ (x+a)(y+b)\equiv\lambda\ (\textnormal{mod }c)\end{subarray}}1\ll_{\varepsilon}(ct)^{\varepsilon}Z(t),

by the divisor bound. On the other hand, if (x,y)∈S⁡(a,b)(x,y)\in S(a,b) satisfies n⁡(z)=(t​x+a′)​(t​y+b′)=0n(z)=(tx+a^{\prime})(ty+b^{\prime})=0, this forces t​x=−a′tx=-a^{\prime} or t​y=−b′ty=-b^{\prime}, determining one of xx and yy uniquely. Suppose xx is determined; the condition c|(x+a)​(y+b)−λc\mid(x+a)(y+b)-\lambda implies d:=gcd⁡(x+a,c)|gcd⁡(λ,c)d:=\gcd(x+a,c)\mid\gcd(\lambda,c), so

cd|x+ad​(y+b)−λd.\frac{c}{d}\ \bigg|\ \frac{x+a}{d}(y+b)-\frac{\lambda}{d}.

Since gcd⁡(c/d,(x+a)/d)=1\gcd(c/d,(x+a)/d)=1, this uniquely determines the value of y⁡(mod ​c/d)y\ (\textnormal{mod }c/d), leading to a total contribution of 1+Y​d/c1+Yd/c. Putting things together, we conclude that

#​S​(a,b)\displaystyle\#S(a,b) ≪εcεmint∈ℤ+(tεZ(t))+1+X+Ycgcd(λ,c)\displaystyle\ll_{\varepsilon}c^{\varepsilon}\min_{t\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}}\left(t^{\varepsilon}Z(t)\right)+1+\frac{X+Y}{c}\gcd(\lambda,c)
≪cε​(X​Yc​mint∈ℤ+​tε​(t+cX​‖a​tc‖+cY​‖b​tc‖)+1+X+Yc​gcd⁡(λ,c))\displaystyle\ll c^{\varepsilon}\left(\frac{XY}{c}\min_{t\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}}t^{\varepsilon}\left(t+\frac{c}{X}\left\|\frac{at}{c}\right\|+\frac{c}{Y}\left\|\frac{bt}{c}\right\|\right)+1+\frac{X+Y}{c}\gcd(\lambda,c)\right)
≪c2​ε​(X​Yc​TcX,cY​(ac,bc)+gcd⁡(λ,c)),\displaystyle\ll c^{2\varepsilon}\left(\frac{XY}{c}T_{\frac{c}{X},\frac{c}{Y}}\left(\frac{a}{c},\frac{b}{c}\right)+\gcd(\lambda,c)\right),

where we used that X,Y≪cX,Y\ll c in the last line (and implicitly that the minimum of t+cX​‖a​t/c‖+cY​‖b​t/c‖t+\frac{c}{X}\|at/c\|+\frac{c}{Y}\|bt/c\| is attained for t≪ct\ll c). Now if α,β∈ℝ\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb{R} satisfy (c​α,c​β)∈I×J(c\alpha,c\beta)\in I\times J, then we have |a−c​α|≤X|a-c\alpha|\leq X and |b−c​β|≤Y|b-c\beta|\leq Y, i.e.,

|ac−α|≤Xc,|bc−β|≤Yc.\left|\frac{a}{c}-\alpha\right|\leq\frac{X}{c},\qquad\qquad\left|\frac{b}{c}-\beta\right|\leq\frac{Y}{c}.

So by 4.4, we have

TcX,cY​(ac,bc)≍TcX,cY​(α,β).T_{\frac{c}{X},\frac{c}{Y}}\left(\frac{a}{c},\frac{b}{c}\right)\asymp T_{\frac{c}{X},\frac{c}{Y}}(\alpha,\beta).

We thus obtain the desired bound, up to a rescaling of ε\varepsilon. ∎

We now work towards our bilinear Kloosterman bound for sequences with sparse Fourier transforms, reminding the reader of the Fourier-analytic notation in Section 3.1. The connection to counting solutions to congruences of the form x​y≡1​(mod ​c)xy\equiv 1\ (\textnormal{mod }c) comes from the identity

(4.8) ∑mam​∑nbn​S​(m,n,c)=∑x,y⁡(mod ​c)a^​(xc)​b^​(yc)​𝟙x​y≡1​(mod ​c),\sum_{m}a_{m}\sum_{n}b_{n}\,S(m,n;c)=\sum_{x,y\ (\textnormal{mod }c)}\widehat{a}\left(\frac{x}{c}\right)\widehat{b}\left(\frac{y}{c}\right)\mathbbm{1}_{xy\equiv 1\ (\textnormal{mod }c)},

obtained by expanding S⁡(m,n,c)S(m,n;c) and swapping sums. One can interpret this as a Parseval–Plancherel identity, the Kloosterman sum S⁡(m,n,c)S(m,n;c) being dual to the function 𝟙x​y≡1​(mod ​c)\mathbbm{1}_{xy\equiv 1\ (\textnormal{mod }c)}; this duality is often exploited in the converse direction (see, e.g., [35, Chapter 6] and [17]), but it turns out to also be a useful input for methods from the spectral theory of automorphic forms.

Proposition 9 (Bilinear Kloosterman bound with exponential phases).

Let c,a∈ℤ+c,a\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}, α,β∈ℝ/ℤ\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}, 1≪M,N≪c1\ll M,N\ll c, and I,J⊂ℤI,J\subset\mathbb{Z} be nonempty discrete intervals of lengths |I|=M|I|=M, |J|=N|J|=N. Then for any ε>0\varepsilon>0, one has

∑m∈Ie(mα)∑n∈Je(nβ)S(am,an;c)≪εcε(cTM,N(α,β)+gcd(a,c)MN).\sum_{m\in I}e(m\alpha)\sum_{n\in J}e(n\beta)\,S(am,an;c)\ll_{\varepsilon}c^{\varepsilon}\left(c\,T_{M,N}(\alpha,\beta)+\gcd(a,c)MN\right).
Remark.

When α=β=0\alpha=\beta=0, this recovers a result of Shparlinski and Zhang [43]. A similar argument produces the more general bound

∑m∈Ie(mα)∑n∈Je(nβ)S(am+r,bn+s;c)≪εcε(cTM,N(α,β)+gcd(a​bgcd⁡(a,b,c),c)MN),\sum_{m\in I}e(m\alpha)\sum_{n\in J}e(n\beta)\,S(am+r,bn+s;c)\ll_{\varepsilon}c^{\varepsilon}\left(c\,T_{M,N}(\alpha,\beta)+\gcd\left(\frac{ab}{\gcd(a,b,c)},c\right)MN\right),

for entries of Kloosterman sums in arithmetic progressions, where a,b∈ℤ∖{0}a,b\in\mathbb{Z}\setminus\{0\}, r,s∈ℤr,s\in\mathbb{Z}.

Proof.

We first note that if gcd⁡(a,c)>1\gcd(a,c)>1 and a′:=a/gcd⁡(a,c)a^{\prime}:=a/\gcd(a,c), c′:=c/gcd⁡(a,c)c^{\prime}:=c/\gcd(a,c), the Chinese remainder theorem yields S⁡(a​m,a​n,c)=φ⁡(c)φ⁡(c′)​S​(a′​m,a′​n,c′)S(am,an;c)=\frac{\varphi(c)}{\varphi(c^{\prime})}S(a^{\prime}m,a^{\prime}n;c^{\prime}). Since φ⁡(c)φ⁡(c′)≤cc′=gcd⁡(a,c)\frac{\varphi(c)}{\varphi(c^{\prime})}\leq\frac{c}{c^{\prime}}=\gcd(a,c), one can deduce the desired bound from the same bound for (a,c)↦(a′,c′)(a,c)\mapsto(a^{\prime},c^{\prime}). This allows us to assume without loss of generality that gcd⁡(a,c)=1\gcd(a,c)=1.

Let 𝒮\mathcal{S} denote the sum in Proposition 9; as in 4.8, we expand S⁡(a​m,a​n,c)S(am,an;c) and swap sums to obtain

𝒮=∑x∈(ℤ/c​ℤ)×∑m∈Ie⁡(m​α+m​a​xc)​∑n∈Je⁡(n​β+n​a​x¯c).\mathcal{S}=\sum_{x\in(\mathbb{Z}/c\mathbb{Z})^{\times}}\sum_{m\in I}e\left(m\alpha+m\frac{ax}{c}\right)\sum_{n\in J}e\left(n\beta+n\frac{a\overline{x}}{c}\right).

We note that

∑m∈Ie⁡(m​α+m​a​xc)≪min⁡(M,‖α+a​xc‖−1),\sum_{m\in I}e\left(m\alpha+m\frac{ax}{c}\right)\ll\min\left(M,\left\|\alpha+\frac{ax}{c}\right\|^{-1}\right),

and put M​‖α+a​xc‖M\|\alpha+\tfrac{ax}{c}\| into dyadic ranges

A0:=[0,2],Aj:=(2j,2j+1].A_{0}:=\left[0,2\right],\qquad\qquad A_{j}:=\left(2^{j},2^{j+1}\right].

Proceeding similarly for the sum over nn, we obtain

𝒮\displaystyle\mathcal{S} =∑0≤j≤log2⁡M0≤k≤log2⁡N∑x∈(ℤ/c​ℤ)×M​‖α+a​xc‖∈AjN​‖β+a​x¯c‖∈Ak∑m∈Ie⁡(m​α+m​a​xc)​∑n∈Je⁡(n​β+n​a​x¯c)\displaystyle=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}0\leq j\leq\log_{2}M\\ 0\leq k\leq\log_{2}N\end{subarray}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}x\in(\mathbb{Z}/c\mathbb{Z})^{\times}\\ M\|\alpha+\frac{ax}{c}\|\in A_{j}\\ N\|\beta+\frac{a\overline{x}}{c}\|\in A_{k}\end{subarray}}\sum_{m\in I}e\left(m\alpha+m\frac{ax}{c}\right)\sum_{n\in J}e\left(n\beta+n\frac{a\overline{x}}{c}\right)
≪∑0≤j≤log2⁡M0≤k≤log2⁡N∑x∈(ℤ/c​ℤ)×𝟙M​‖α+a​xc‖∈Aj​𝟙N​‖β+a​x¯c‖∈Ak​M​N2j+k\displaystyle\ll\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}0\leq j\leq\log_{2}M\\ 0\leq k\leq\log_{2}N\end{subarray}}\sum_{x\in(\mathbb{Z}/c\mathbb{Z})^{\times}}\mathbbm{1}_{M\|\alpha+\frac{ax}{c}\|\in A_{j}}\mathbbm{1}_{N\|\beta+\frac{a\overline{x}}{c}\|\in A_{k}}\,\frac{MN}{2^{j+k}}
≤∑0≤j≤log2⁡M0≤k≤log2⁡NM​N2j+k​∑x,y∈ℤ/c​ℤx​y≡a2​(mod ​c)𝟙M​‖α+xc‖∈Aj​ 1N​‖β+yc‖∈Ak.\displaystyle\leq\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}0\leq j\leq\log_{2}M\\ 0\leq k\leq\log_{2}N\end{subarray}}\frac{MN}{2^{j+k}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}x,y\in\mathbb{Z}/c\mathbb{Z}\\ xy\equiv a^{2}\ (\textnormal{mod }c)\end{subarray}}\mathbbm{1}_{M\|\alpha+\frac{x}{c}\|\in A_{j}}\,\mathbbm{1}_{N\|\beta+\frac{y}{c}\|\in A_{k}}.
≤∑0≤j≤log2⁡M0≤k≤log2⁡NM​N2j+k​∑x,y∈ℤx​y≡a2​(mod ​c)𝟙|x+c​α|≤c​2j+1M​ 1|y+c​β|≤c​2k+1N,\displaystyle\leq\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}0\leq j\leq\log_{2}M\\ 0\leq k\leq\log_{2}N\end{subarray}}\frac{MN}{2^{j+k}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}x,y\in\mathbb{Z}\\ xy\equiv a^{2}\ (\textnormal{mod }c)\end{subarray}}\mathbbm{1}_{|x+c\alpha|\leq c\frac{2^{j+1}}{M}}\,\mathbbm{1}_{|y+c\beta|\leq c\frac{2^{k+1}}{N}},

where we noted that for any x0,y0∈ℤ/c​ℤx_{0},y_{0}\in\mathbb{Z}/c\mathbb{Z}, there exist x,y∈ℤx,y\in\mathbb{Z} with x≡x0​(mod ​c)x\equiv x_{0}\ (\textnormal{mod }c), y≡y0​(mod ​c)y\equiv y_{0}\ (\textnormal{mod }c), and ‖α+x0c‖=|α+xc|\|\alpha+\frac{x_{0}}{c}\|=|\alpha+\frac{x}{c}|, ‖β+y0c‖=|β+yc|\|\beta+\frac{y_{0}}{c}\|=|\beta+\frac{y}{c}|.

We can bound the inner sum using Lemma 8 with X=c​2j+2​M−1X=c2^{j+2}M^{-1}, Y=c​2k+2​N−1Y=c2^{k+2}N^{-1}, and λ=a2\lambda=a^{2}. Since the function TM,NT_{M,N} is non-decreasing in M,NM,N, this gives

𝒮\displaystyle\mathcal{S} ≪εcε∑0≤j≤log2⁡M0≤k≤log2⁡NM​N2j+k((c​2j​M−1)​(c​2k​N−1)cTM2j+1,N2k+1(−α,−β)+gcd(a2,c))\displaystyle\ll_{\varepsilon}c^{\varepsilon}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}0\leq j\leq\log_{2}M\\ 0\leq k\leq\log_{2}N\end{subarray}}\frac{MN}{2^{j+k}}\left(\frac{(c2^{j}M^{-1})(c2^{k}N^{-1})}{c}T_{\frac{M}{2^{j+1}},\frac{N}{2^{k+1}}}\left(-\alpha,-\beta\right)+\gcd(a^{2},c)\right)
≪εc2​ε(cTM,N(α,β)+MN).\displaystyle\ll_{\varepsilon}c^{2\varepsilon}\left(cT_{M,N}\left(\alpha,\beta\right)+MN\right).

This yields the desired bound up to a rescaling of ε\varepsilon. ∎

Proposition 10 (Bilinear Kloosterman bound with frequency concentration).

Let c,a∈ℤ+c,a\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}, 1≪M,N≪c1\ll M,N\ll c, and I,J⊂ℤI,J\subset\mathbb{Z} be nonempty discrete intervals of lengths |I|=M|I|=M, |J|=N|J|=N. Then for any ε>0\varepsilon>0, one has

(4.9) ∑m∈Iam∑n∈JbnS(am,an;c)≪εcε∬(ℝ/ℤ)2(cTM,N(α,β)+gcd(a,c)MN)d|μ|(α)d|ν|(β),\sum_{m\in I}a_{m}\sum_{n\in J}b_{n}\,S(am,an;c)\ll_{\varepsilon}c^{\varepsilon}\iint_{(\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z})^{2}}\left(c\,T_{M,N}(\alpha,\beta)+\gcd(a,c)MN\right)d|\mu|(\alpha)\,d|\nu|(\beta),

By 4.5, when M=NM=N, this bound is ≪cε​(c​N2/3+gcd⁡(a,c)​N2)​|μ|​(ℝ/ℤ)​|ν|​(ℝ/ℤ)\ll c^{\varepsilon}(cN^{2/3}+\gcd(a,c)N^{2})\,|\mu|(\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z})\,|\nu|(\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}).

Proof.

By Fourier inversion, expand

am=∫ℝ/ℤe⁡(m​α)​𝑑μ​(α),bn=∫ℝ/ℤe⁡(n​β)​𝑑μ​(β),a_{m}=\int_{\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}}e(m\alpha)\,d\mu(\alpha),\qquad\qquad b_{n}=\int_{\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}}e(n\beta)\,d\mu(\beta),

then swap sums and integrals, and apply Proposition 9. ∎

Remark.

Suppose M=NM=N and a=1a=1. By comparison, the pointwise Weil bound would yield a right-hand side in 4.9 of roughly N​c​‖am‖2​‖bn‖2N\sqrt{c}\,\|a_{m}\|_{2}\|b_{n}\|_{2}, while applying Cauchy–Schwarz after 4.8 gives the bound c​‖am‖2​‖bn‖2c\|a_{m}\|_{2}\|b_{n}\|_{2} (these essentially lead to the ranges in Theorem A). It is a very difficult problem [29, 27] to improve these bounds for general sequences (am),(bn)(a_{m}),(b_{n}), but it becomes easier given suitable information in the frequency space. Indeed, with the natural choice of measures d​μ=a^​d​λd\mu=\widehat{a}\,d\lambda, d​ν=b^​d​λd\nu=\widehat{b}\,d\lambda (where λ\lambda is the Lebesgue measure), Proposition 10 saves over the relevant bound c​‖am‖2​‖bn‖2=c​‖a^‖L2​‖b^‖L2c\|a_{m}\|_{2}\|b_{n}\|_{2}=c\|\widehat{a}\|_{L^{2}}\|\widehat{b}\|_{L^{2}} whenever a^,b^\widehat{a},\widehat{b} satisfy the concentration inequality

‖a^‖L1‖a^‖L2⋅‖b^‖L1‖b^‖L2=o⁡(1N2/3+N2​c−1).\frac{\|\widehat{a}\|_{L^{1}}}{\|\widehat{a}\|_{L^{2}}}\cdot\frac{\|\widehat{b}\|_{L^{1}}}{\|\widehat{b}\|_{L^{2}}}=o\left(\frac{1}{N^{2/3}+N^{2}c^{-1}}\right).

For reference, the left-hand side is always ≫N−1\gg N^{-1}. One may do better by treating the integral in 4.9 more carefully, or by including the contribution of other frequencies into μ\mu and ν\nu (this liberty is due to the handling of sharp cutoffs in Proposition 9). For instance, one could extend the sequences (am),(bn)(a_{m}),(b_{n}) with a smooth decay beyond II and JJ before taking their Fourier transforms, or one could construct μ,ν\mu,\nu out of Dirac delta measures (in particular, one recovers Proposition 9 this way).

We will ultimately use Proposition 10 for sequences (an)(a_{n}) of the shape in 1.3, so it is necessary to understand their Fourier transforms. The case of exponential phases an=e⁡(n​α)a_{n}=e(n\alpha) is trivial, but the dispersion coefficients from Theorem 3 are more interesting, warranting a separate lemma.
