Remark.

As in [42], the arguments in this subsection extend immediately to sums of weighted Kloosterman sums

Sw​(m,n,c):=∑x∈(ℤ/c​ℤ)×w⁡(x)​e​(m​x+n​x¯c),S_{w}(m,n;c):=\sum_{x\in(\mathbb{Z}/c\mathbb{Z})^{\times}}w(x)\,e\left(\frac{mx+n\overline{x}}{c}\right),

for arbitrary 11-bounded coefficients w⁡(x)w(x). In particular, choosing w⁡(x)w(x) in terms of a Dirichlet character χ\chi mod q0q_{0}, where q0​∣q∣​cq_{0}\mid q\mid c, should ultimately extend our large sieve inequalities to the exceptional Maass forms of level qq associated to a general nebentypus χ\chi, rather than the trivial one.

5. Spectral bounds

We now combine the combinatorial arguments from the previous section with techniques from the spectral theory of automorphic forms (inspired by [9]), to prove new large sieve inequalities for exceptional Maass cusp forms, and then to deduce bounds for multilinear forms of Kloosterman sums. The reader should be familiar with the prerequisites in all of Section 3, especially Section 3.4.

5.1. A general large sieve for exceptional Maass forms

Our common generalization of Theorems 2 and 3 requires the following notation, applied to the Fourier transform of a sequence (an)(a_{n}).

Given N≥1/2N\geq 1/2 and a bounded-variation complex Borel measure μ\mu on ℝ/ℤ\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}, we denote

5.2. Proofs of Theorems 2 and 3

We can now deduce the large sieve inequalities promised in Section 1.1, starting from Theorem 13.

from 1.7. In particular, we can recall from 4.5 that TN​(α,α)≪NT_{N}(\alpha,\alpha)\ll\sqrt{N}, so this includes the range X≪(N,qa​N)X\ll(\sqrt{N},\tfrac{q}{a\sqrt{N}}) uniformly in α\alpha. 5.3. Multilinear Kloosterman bounds

In contrast to the “vertical” bilinear averages of Kloosterman sums S⁡(m,n,c)S(m,n;c) over m,nm,n from Section 4 (or from [29, 27]), the bounds in this subsection also require “horizontal” averaging over the modulus cc—crucially, with a smooth weight in this variable. Generally, it is such horizontal averages that make use of the Kuznetsov trace formula for Γ0​(q)\Gamma_{0}(q), leading to dependencies on the spectral parameter θ⁡(q)=max⁡(0,14−λ1​(q))≤764\theta(q)=\sqrt{\max(0,\tfrac{1}{4}-\lambda_{1}(q))}\leq\tfrac{7}{64}; we recall that the purpose of large sieve inequalities for the exceptional spectrum, like Theorem 13, is to improve the dependency on θ⁡(q)\theta(q).

Throughout this subsection, we will work with sequences obeying the following condition.

Assumption 14 (Large sieve for the tuple (q,N,Z,(an)n∼N,AN,YN)(q,N,Z,(a_{n})_{n\sim N},A_{N},Y_{N})).

This applies to complex sequences (an)n∼N(a_{n})_{n\sim N} and parameters q∈ℤ+q\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}, N≥1/2N\geq 1/2, Z≫1Z\gg 1, AN≫‖an‖2A_{N}\gg\|a_{n}\|_{2}, YN>0Y_{N}>0. For any ε>0,ξ∈ℝ\varepsilon>0,\xi\in\mathbb{R}, any cusp 𝔞\mathfrak{a} of Γ0​(q)\Gamma_{0}(q) with μ⁡(𝔞)=q−1\mu(\mathfrak{a})=q^{-1} and σ𝔞\sigma_{\mathfrak{a}} chosen as in 3.9, and any orthonormal basis of Maass cusp forms for Γ0​(q)\Gamma_{0}(q), with eigenvalues λj\lambda_{j} and Fourier coefficients ρj​𝔞​(n)\rho_{j\mathfrak{a}}(n), one has

(5.17) ∑λj<1/4X2​θj|∑n∼Ne(nNξ)anρj​𝔞(n)|2≪ε(qNZ)ε(1+Nq)AN2,\sum_{\lambda_{j}<1/4}X^{2\theta_{j}}\left|\sum_{n\sim N}e\left(\frac{n}{N}\xi\right)a_{n}\,\rho_{j\mathfrak{a}}(n)\right|^{2}\ll_{\varepsilon}(qNZ)^{\varepsilon}\left(1+\frac{N}{q}\right)A_{N}^{2},

for all X≪max⁡(1,qN)​YN1+|ξ|2X\ll\max\left(1,\frac{q}{N}\right)\frac{Y_{N}}{1+|\xi|^{2}}.

For example, Theorem A shows that the tuple (q,N,1,(an)n∼N,‖an‖22,1)(q,N,1,(a_{n})_{n\sim N},\|a_{n}\|_{2}^{2},1) satisfies Assumption 14 for any q∈ℤ+q\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}, N≥1/2N\geq 1/2 and any complex sequence (an)n∼N(a_{n})_{n\sim N}; attaining higher values of YNY_{N} requires more information about (an)(a_{n}). for any α∈ℝ/ℤ\alpha\in\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z} and q∈ℤ+q\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}, N≥1/2N\geq 1/2, Z=1Z=1; note that the phase ξ/N\xi/N can be incorporated into α\alpha, and we implicitly used that TN​(α+ξ/N)≪(1+|ξ|2)​TN​(α)T_{N}(\alpha+\xi/N)\ll(1+|\xi|^{2})\,T_{N}(\alpha) by 4.3. Likewise, incorporating ℓi​ξ/N\ell_{i}\xi/N into αi\alpha_{i}, Theorem 3 shows that we can choose

(5.19) an:=∑h1,h2∈ℤh1​ℓ1−h2​ℓ2=nΦ1​(h1H)​Φ2​(h2H)​e​(h1​α1+h2​α2),YN:=max(1,N​H(H+L)​L​mini​TH​(αi)),AN:=∥an∥2+NHL+H2L2,\begin{gathered}a_{n}:=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}h_{1},h_{2}\in\mathbb{Z}\\ h_{1}\ell_{1}-h_{2}\ell_{2}=n\end{subarray}}\Phi_{1}\left(\frac{h_{1}}{H}\right)\Phi_{2}\left(\frac{h_{2}}{H}\right)e(h_{1}\alpha_{1}+h_{2}\alpha_{2}),\\ Y_{N}:=\max\left(1,\frac{NH}{(H+L)L\min_{i}T_{H}(\alpha_{i})}\right),\qquad A_{N}:=\|a_{n}\|_{2}+\sqrt{N}\sqrt{\frac{H}{L}+\frac{H^{2}}{L^{2}}},\end{gathered}

where 1≪L2≪q1\ll L^{2}\ll q, 1≪H≪Z1\ll H\ll Z, αi∈ℝ/ℤ\alpha_{i}\in\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}, ℓi≍L\ell_{i}\asymp L, (ℓ1,ℓ2)=1(\ell_{1},\ell_{2})=1, and Φi​(t)\Phi_{i}(t) are smooth functions supported in t≪1t\ll 1 with Φi(j)≪j1\Phi_{i}^{(j)}\ll_{j}1. for

T=T0YN,T0:=Cmax⁡(m,q2​(q,m)−1)1/2​max⁡(N,q)1/2≤Cq3/2(q,m)−1/2.T=\frac{T_{0}}{\sqrt{Y_{N}}},\qquad\qquad T_{0}:=\frac{C}{\max\left(m,q^{2}(q,m)^{-1}\right)^{1/2}\max\left(N,q\right)^{1/2}}\leq\frac{C}{q^{3/2}(q,m)^{-1/2}}.
Remark.

The parameter T0T_{0} indicates the best known dependency on θ=θ⁡(q)\theta=\theta(q) that one could achieve without our large sieve inequalities; for example, when an=e⁡(n​α)a_{n}=e(n\alpha) and YN=NY_{N}=\sqrt{N}, Corollary 15 saves a total factor of Nθ/2N^{\theta/2} over previous bounds (and up to NθN^{\theta} if α\alpha is close to a rational number of small denominator). We note that in practice, the second term in each maximum from T0T_{0} is usually dominant, and the factors in the second line of 5.20 are typically ≍1\asymp 1.

Remark.

While the smooth weight in the cc variable is necessary here (stemming from Proposition E), the smooth weight in nn only confers additional flexibility. Indeed, one can take Φ⁡(x,y)=f⁡(x)​g​(y)\Phi(x,y)=f(x)g(y) for compactly-supported functions f,g:(0,∞)→ℂf,g:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb{C}, where f≡1f\equiv 1 on (1,2)(1,2); this effectively replaces Φ⁡(n/N,c/C)\Phi(n/N,c/C) with g⁡(c/C)g(c/C) in 5.20. The same remark applies to the next results.

6. The greatest prime factor of n2+1n^{2}+1

Here we use our new inputs from Section 5.3 in the computations of Merikoski [37] and de la Bretèche–Drappeau [8], in order to prove Theorem 1. We begin with a brief informal sketch.

6.1. Sketch of the argument

We will ultimately prove a lower bound of the shape

∑n∼x∑p​ primep|n2+1p>x1.3log⁡p>ε​x​log⁡x,\sum_{n\sim x}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}p\text{ prime}\\ p\mid n^{2}+1\\ p>x^{1.3}\end{subarray}}\log p>\varepsilon\,x\log x,

which implies that for some (in fact, for many) n∼xn\sim x, we must have P+​(n2+1)>x1.3P^{+}(n^{2}+1)>x^{1.3}. As in previous works [37, 8, 10, 23], we use an idea of Chebyshev to estimate the full sum

∑n∼x∑p​ primep|n2+1log⁡p≈∑n∼x∑d|n2+1Λ⁡(d)=∑n∼xlog⁡(n2+1)=2​x​log​x+O⁡(x),\sum_{n\sim x}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}p\text{ prime}\\ p\mid n^{2}+1\end{subarray}}\log p\approx\sum_{n\sim x}\sum_{d\mid n^{2}+1}\Lambda(d)=\sum_{n\sim x}\log(n^{2}+1)=2x\log x+O(x),

where Λ\Lambda is the von Mangoldt function. It then remains to upper bound

∑n∼x∑p​ primep|n2+1p≤x1.3log⁡p=∑p​ primep≤x1.3log⁡p​∑n∼x𝟙n2≡−1​(mod ​p)<?(2−ε)​x​log⁡x.\sum_{n\sim x}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}p\text{ prime}\\ p\mid n^{2}+1\\ p\leq x^{1.3}\end{subarray}}\log p=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}p\text{ prime}\\ p\leq x^{1.3}\end{subarray}}\log p\,\sum_{n\sim x}\mathbbm{1}_{n^{2}\equiv-1\ (\textnormal{mod }p)}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle?}}{{<}}(2-\varepsilon)\,x\log x.

Following Merikoski [37], we use repeated applications of Buchstab’s identity inside the Harman sieve method, to reduce estimating the above sum over primes to bounding “Type I” and “Type II” sums of the form

∑d≤Dλd​∑q∼Qq≡0​(mod ​d)(∑n∼x𝟙n2≡−1​(mod ​q)−xq​∑ν⁡(mod ​q)𝟙ν2≡−1​(mod ​q)),\sum_{d\leq D}\lambda_{d}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}q\sim Q\\ q\equiv 0\ (\textnormal{mod }d)\end{subarray}}\left(\sum_{n\sim x}\mathbbm{1}_{n^{2}\equiv-1\ (\textnormal{mod }q)}-\frac{x}{q}\sum_{\nu\ (\textnormal{mod }q)}\mathbbm{1}_{\nu^{2}\equiv-1\ (\textnormal{mod }q)}\right),

respectively

∑q1∼Q1λq1​∑q2∼Q2μq2​(∑n∼x𝟙n2≡−1​(mod ​q1​q2)−xq1​q2​∑ν⁡(mod ​q1​q2)𝟙ν2≡−1​(mod ​q1​q2)),\sum_{q_{1}\sim Q_{1}}\lambda_{q_{1}}\sum_{q_{2}\sim Q_{2}}\mu_{q_{2}}\left(\sum_{n\sim x}\mathbbm{1}_{n^{2}\equiv-1\ (\textnormal{mod }q_{1}q_{2})}-\frac{x}{q_{1}q_{2}}\sum_{\nu\ (\textnormal{mod }q_{1}q_{2})}\mathbbm{1}_{\nu^{2}\equiv-1\ (\textnormal{mod }q_{1}q_{2})}\right),

for various ranges of D,Q,QiD,Q,Q_{i} with Q1​Q2=Q≤x1.3Q_{1}Q_{2}=Q\leq x^{1.3}, aiming to win over the trivial bound of xx.

Let us sketch our improvement of the Type I information. As in [8, 37], we separate nn into residue classes ν⁡(mod ​q)\nu\ (\textnormal{mod }q) and apply a truncated version of Poisson summation to the sum over nn; the principal frequency h=0h=0 cancels with the subtracted main term, leading to a sum like

∑d≤Dλd​∑q∼Qq≡0​(mod ​d)∑ν⁡(mod ​q)ν2≡−1​(q)∑h∼Qxe⁡(h​νq).\sum_{d\leq D}\lambda_{d}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}q\sim Q\\ q\equiv 0\ (\textnormal{mod }d)\end{subarray}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\nu\ (\textnormal{mod }q)\\ \nu^{2}\equiv-1\ (q)\end{subarray}}\ \sum_{h\sim\frac{Q}{x}}e\left(\frac{h\nu}{q}\right).

We can then parametrize the solutions to ν2≡−1​(mod ​q)\nu^{2}\equiv-1\ (\textnormal{mod }q) by the Gauss correspondence (see [10, Lemma 2]), which gives q=r2+s2q=r^{2}+s^{2} and νq≈r¯s​(mod ​1)\tfrac{\nu}{q}\approx\tfrac{\overline{r}}{s}\ (\textnormal{mod }1). In the critical range r,s∼Qr,s\sim\sqrt{Q}, this leaves us with the sum

∑d≤Dλd​∑r,s∼Qr2≡−s2​(mod ​d)∑h∼Qxe⁡(h​r¯s).\sum_{d\leq D}\lambda_{d}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}r,s\sim\sqrt{Q}\\ r^{2}\equiv-s^{2}\ (\textnormal{mod }d)\end{subarray}}\sum_{h\sim\frac{Q}{x}}e\left(\frac{h\overline{r}}{s}\right).

Separating r​s¯r\overline{s} into residue classes ϱ​mod ​d\varrho\ \textnormal{mod }d and Fourier-completing the sum over rr yields a dual variable kk of size DD, and inner sums of the shape

∑k∼D∑h∼Qxe⁡(k​ϱd)​∑s∼QS⁡(h,k​d¯,s),\sum_{k\sim D}\sum_{h\sim\frac{Q}{x}}e\left(\frac{k\varrho}{d}\right)\sum_{s\sim\sqrt{Q}}S(h,k\overline{d};s),

where ϱ\varrho is a solution to ϱ2≡−1​(mod ​d)\varrho^{2}\equiv-1\ (\textnormal{mod }d); compare these to 1.2. Since the sequence (e⁡(k​ϱd))k∼D(e(\tfrac{k\varrho}{d}))_{k\sim D} depends on the level dd and its length is as large as the level, the large sieve inequality for general sequences from Theorem A cannot produce any savings in the XθX^{\theta}-aspect for this sequence. However, our large sieve inequality for exponential phases from Theorem 2 will save a factor of Dθ/2D^{\theta/2}, which follows through to the sieve computations. This improves the results of de la Bretèche–Drappeau [8, §8], based in turn on Duke–Friedlander–Iwaniec [16], and is nearly enough to remove the dependency on Selberg’s eigenvalue conjecture in the relevant Type I ranges, as illustrated in Figure 2 (left).

Following Merikoski [37], the Type II sums can be treated similarly using an additional Cauchy–Schwarz step. Once again, this leads to trilinear forms of Kloosterman sums as in 1.2, where both sequences (am)(a_{m}) and (bn)(b_{n}) depend on the level. Using our large sieve inequalities, we can leverage the fact that (am)(a_{m}) happen to be exponential phases as in Theorem 2, while (bn)(b_{n}) have the shape in Theorem 3 (if the sum over hh is kept inside the Cauchy–Schwarz step). This ultimately produces three admissible Type II ranges, all gathered in Proposition 22 and illustrated in Figure 2 (right).

By carefully plugging in these Type I and II estimates into Merikoski’s Harman sieve computations, which require the numerical calculation of multidimensional integrals, we deduce Theorem 1.

This is a refinement of the first and third bounds in [8, Lemme 8.3], winning factors of about qθ/2q^{\theta/2} via our Corollaries 15 and 17. We only mention what changes from the proof in [8, §8.1], working in the particular case d=r=1d=r=1, D=−1D=-1. We note that for D=−1D=-1, the relevant cusps 𝔞\mathfrak{a} from [8, §8.1] are equivalent to 0/10/1, and thus have μ⁡(𝔞)=q−1\mu(\mathfrak{a})=q^{-1} (which is also why Merikoski’s bounds in [37, §3.8] only require such cusps too).

For part (i)(i), we consider the sums of Kloosterman sums from [8, (8.30)], given (with notation to be explained below) by

VN=VN​(q,h):=∑N/2≤|n|≤2​N∑γ∈𝒞∞​𝔞S∞​𝔞​(h,n,γ)​GN​(γ,n).V_{N}=V_{N}(q,h):=\sum_{N/2\leq|n|\leq 2N}\sum_{\gamma\in\mathcal{C}_{\infty\mathfrak{a}}}S_{\infty\mathfrak{a}}(h,n;\gamma)\,G_{N}(\gamma,n).

Also, 𝔞\mathfrak{a} is a cusp of Γ0​(q)\Gamma_{0}(q), and the scaling matrix σ𝔞\sigma_{\mathfrak{a}} used implicitly in the Kloosterman sum S∞​𝔞​(h,n,γ)S_{\infty\mathfrak{a}}(h,n;\gamma) hides an exponential phase of the form e⁡(n​αq)e(n\alpha_{q}); the value of αq\alpha_{q} is arbitrary for our purposes.

We can now apply Corollary 15 (equivalently, we can bound ℳNexc\mathscr{M}_{N}^{\textnormal{exc}} in [8, (8.40)] using Theorem 2), using an=e⁡(n​αq)a_{n}=e(n\alpha_{q}), YN=AN=NY_{N}=A_{N}=\sqrt{N} (corresponding to 5.18), C=q​MC=q\sqrt{M}, and m=|h|m=|h|. This yields

VN≪η(qhM)O⁡(η)(1+q​Mq3/2(q,h)−1/2N1/4)2​θN​M,V_{N}\ll_{\eta}(qhM)^{O(\eta)}\left(1+\frac{q\sqrt{M}}{q^{3/2}(q,h)^{-1/2}N^{1/4}}\right)^{2\theta}\sqrt{NM},

where we used that qη​C=q1+η​M≫h​Nq^{\eta}C=q^{1+\eta}\sqrt{M}\gg\sqrt{hN}, that (q,h)​|h|≤|h|≤q\sqrt{(q,h)|h|}\leq|h|\leq q, and that N≪q1+η​MηN\ll q^{1+\eta}M^{\eta} (in particular, the 11-term is dominant in the last two parentheses from 1.1, up to factors of (q​h​M)o⁡(1)(qhM)^{o(1)}).

which gives the second term claimed in the upper bound from 6.1.

Part (i​i)(ii) follows similarly using Corollary 17 (or equivalently, by bounding ℳNexc\mathscr{M}_{N}^{\textnormal{exc}} in [8, §8.1.12] using Theorem 2 once again). Indeed, with the similar choices an,q=e⁡(n​αq)a_{n,q}=e(n\alpha_{q}), YN=AN,q=NY_{N}=A_{N,q}=\sqrt{N}, Z=Q​MZ=QM, and C=Q​MC=Q\sqrt{M}, our bound 5.31 yields

Notation 20 (Set-up for arithmetic information).

Let x≥1x\geq 1, α∈[1,3/2)\alpha\in[1,3/2), and

P:=xα.P:=x^{\alpha}.

Let Φ,Ψ\Phi,\Psi be smooth functions supported in [1,4][1,4], satisfying Φ≥0\Phi\geq 0 and Φ(j),Ψ(j)≪j1\Phi^{(j)},\Psi^{(j)}\ll_{j}1 for j≥0j\geq 0 (in [37, §2.1], Merikoski uses b⁡(t)=Φ⁡(t/x)b(t)=\Phi(t/x) and Ψ⁡(t)←Ψ⁡(t/P)\Psi(t)\leftarrow\Psi(t/P)). For q∈ℤ+q\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}, define

|𝒜q|:=∑n2≡−1​(mod ​q)Φ⁡(nx),X:=∫Φ⁡(tx)​𝑑t=x​∫Φ,|\mathcal{A}_{q}|:=\sum_{n^{2}\equiv-1\ (\textnormal{mod }q)}\Phi\left(\frac{n}{x}\right),\qquad\qquad X:=\int\Phi\left(\frac{t}{x}\right)\,dt=x\int\Phi,
ρ⁡(q):=#⁡{ν∈ℤ/q​ℤ:ν2≡−1​(mod ​q)}.\rho(q):=\#\left\{\nu\in\mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z}:\nu^{2}\equiv-1\ (\textnormal{mod }q)\right\}.

We will estimate the difference

|𝒜q|−X​ρ⁡(q)q|\mathcal{A}_{q}|-X\frac{\rho(q)}{q}

in “Type I” and “Type II” sums with q≍Pq\asymp P. The Type I sums average over moduli in arithmetic progressions, say q≡0​(mod ​d)q\equiv 0\ (\textnormal{mod }d) and d≤Dd\leq D, with arbitrary divisor-bounded coefficients λd\lambda_{d}; the Type II sums average over moduli with a conveniently-sized factor, say q=m​nq=mn with n∼Nn\sim N (and m≍P/Nm\asymp P/N), with divisor-bounded coefficients am,bna_{m},b_{n}. One can also view the Type I sums as special Type II sums where am=1a_{m}=1, except that Type II estimates typically require a lower bound on NN.

The strength of the resulting Type I and Type II information is given by the ranges of parameters DD and NN (in terms of xx and PP) for which we can obtain power-savings over the trivial bound—i.e., for which the sums over |𝒜q||\mathcal{A}_{q}| have an asymptotic formula. Figure 2 illustrates the (previous unconditional, new unconditional, and conditional) admissible choices of logx⁡D\log_{x}D and logx⁡N\log_{x}N in terms of α=logx⁡P\alpha=\log_{x}P; both graphs continue downwards, the second region being lower-bounded by the function α−1\alpha-1. The previous unconditional and the conditional ranges are due to Merikoski [37] and de la Bretèche–Drappeau [8]; our improvements are Propositions 21 and 22.

Proposition 21 (Type I estimate).

For any sufficiently small ε>0\varepsilon>0 there exists δ>0\delta>0 such that the following holds. With Notation 20, 1≤α≤1.41\leq\alpha\leq 1.4, θ:=764\theta:=\tfrac{7}{64}, and D≥1D\geq 1, one has

(6.3) ∑d≤Dλd∑q≡0​(mod ​d)(|𝒜q|−Xρ⁡(q)q)Ψ(qP)logq≪εx1−δ,\sum_{d\leq D}\lambda_{d}\sum_{q\equiv 0\ (\textnormal{mod }d)}\left(|\mathcal{A}_{q}|-X\frac{\rho(q)}{q}\right)\Psi\left(\frac{q}{P}\right)\log q\ll_{\varepsilon}x^{1-\delta},

for any divisor-bounded coefficients (λd)(\lambda_{d}), provided that

D≪εx−εmin(x1/2,x(1−2​θ​α)/(2−5​θ)).D\ll_{\varepsilon}x^{-\varepsilon}\min\left(x^{1/2},x^{(1-2\theta\alpha)/(2-5\theta)}\right).
Proof.

This is a refinement of Merikoski’s [37, Prop. 1] (which explicitated the computations in de la Bretèche–Drappeau’s [8, §8.4]), using our Lemma 19.(i​i)(ii) instead of [8, (8.7)]. Indeed, in the first display on [8, p. 1620], by applying 6.2 for H←P​X−1+δH\leftarrow PX^{-1+\delta} (for δ=δ⁡(ε)\delta=\delta(\varepsilon) to be chosen shortly), Q←D≤x1/2Q\leftarrow D\leq x^{1/2} and M←P/DM\leftarrow P/D, we instead obtain the bound

RH​(x,P,D)\displaystyle R_{H}(x,P,D)
≪δx1+O⁡(δ)P−1DH(H+PD(1+H−2​θDθ/2(PD)θ)+PH(1+D−3θ/2(PD)θ))\displaystyle\ll_{\delta}x^{1+O(\delta)}P^{-1}DH\left(H+\sqrt{\frac{P}{D}}\left(1+H^{-2\theta}D^{\theta/2}\left(\frac{P}{D}\right)^{\theta}\right)+\sqrt{\frac{P}{H}}\left(1+D^{-3\theta/2}\left(\frac{P}{D}\right)^{\theta}\right)\right)
=xO⁡(δ)(P​Dx+P​D(1+x2​θP−θD−θ/2)+xD(1+D−5θ/2Pθ)).\displaystyle=x^{O(\delta)}\left(\frac{PD}{x}+\sqrt{PD}\left(1+x^{2\theta}P^{-\theta}D^{-\theta/2}\right)+\sqrt{x}D\left(1+D^{-5\theta/2}P^{\theta}\right)\right).

Here, RH​(x,P,D)R_{H}(x,P,D) resulted from our Type I sum after putting dd in dyadic ranges, expanding and Fourier-completing |𝒜q||\mathcal{A}_{q}|; see [8, §8.4] and then [10, §4, 5]. Overall, this bound is acceptable in 6.3 (i.e., ≪εx1−δ\ll_{\varepsilon}x^{1-\delta}) provided that for an absolute constant KK, one has

D\displaystyle D ≪εx−K​δmin(x2P−1,x1/2,x2​(1−2​θ)/(1−θ)P−(1−2θ)/(1−θ),x1/(2−5​θ)P−2θ/(2−5θ))\displaystyle\ll_{\varepsilon}x^{-K\delta}\min\left(x^{2}P^{-1},x^{1/2},x^{2(1-2\theta)/(1-\theta)}P^{-(1-2\theta)/(1-\theta)},x^{1/(2-5\theta)}P^{-2\theta/(2-5\theta)}\right)
=x−ε​min⁡(x2−α,x1/2,x(2−α)​(1−2​θ)/(1−θ),x(1−2​θ​α)/(2−5​θ)),\displaystyle=x^{-\varepsilon}\min\left(x^{2-\alpha},x^{1/2},x^{(2-\alpha)(1-2\theta)/(1-\theta)},x^{(1-2\theta\alpha)/(2-5\theta)}\right),

where we picked δ:=ε/K\delta:=\varepsilon/K and substituted P=xαP=x^{\alpha}. A quick numerical verification shows that for 1≤α≤1.41\leq\alpha\leq 1.4 and θ=764\theta=\tfrac{7}{64}, the first and the third term do not contribute to the minimum. ∎

For any sufficiently small ε>0\varepsilon>0 there exists δ>0\delta>0 such that the following holds. With Notation 20, θ:=764\theta:=\tfrac{7}{64}, and M​N=PMN=P with M,N≥1M,N\geq 1, one has

    (bn)(b_{n}) is supported on square-free integers, and

Remark.

The upper range in Proposition 22.(i​i)(ii), which completely removes the dependency on Selberg’s eigenvalue conjecture, wins over that in Proposition 21.(i)(i) only for α<136/129≈1.054\alpha<136/129\approx 1.054. As in [37], assuming Selberg’s eigenvalue conjecture, the full admissible range in part (i)(i) is N≪εx(2−α)/3N\ll_{\varepsilon}x^{(2-\alpha)/3}, which includes the range in part (i​i)(ii).

Proof of Proposition 22.(i​i)(ii), assuming (i)(i).

This is a refinement of Merikoski’s [37, Prop. 4.(ii)], using our Lemma 19.(i)(i) instead of de la Bretèche–Drappeau’s bound [8, (8.5)].

We briefly recall that in [37, §3], Merikoski expanded and Fourier-completed |𝒜m​n||\mathcal{A}_{mn}| (resulting in a sum over 1≤|h|≤H:=P​x−1+δ1\leq|h|\leq H:=Px^{-1+\delta}), removed the smooth cross-conditions in h,m,nh,m,n, and inserted the condition (m,n)=1(m,n)=1 to reach Type II sums Σ⁡(M,N)\Sigma(M,N). This results in a contribution to Σ⁡(M,N)\Sigma(M,N) of

Trivially removing the first term, picking δ:=ε/K\delta:=\varepsilon/K, and substituting P=xαP=x^{\alpha}, this proves 6.4 in the range

and

Remark.

As in [37, §3.10], the bound for Ξ0​(M,N)\Xi_{0}(M,N) in the proof above does not leverage any cancellation over hh. One can attempt to do this using Corollary 16 with am=e⁡(m​αq)a_{m}=e(m\alpha_{q}) and bnb_{n} as in 1.10, but the gain in the HH-aspect would be smaller than the loss in the θ\theta-aspect in our computations. This is because Proposition 22.(i​i)(ii) is only relevant for α\alpha close to 11, i.e., for small values of HH.

Proof of Proposition 22.(i)(i).

This is a refinement of Merikoski’s [37, Prop. 4.(i)], using Corollary 16 (plus Theorem 3) instead of Deshouillers–Iwaniec’s bound [9, Theorem 9].

We very briefly recall the relevant parts of Merikoski’s argument and the sizes of the parameters therein, pointing the reader to [37, §3] for details. In [37, §3.4], one expanded and Fourier-completed |𝒜m​n||\mathcal{A}_{mn}|, resulting in a sum over 1≤|h|≤H1\leq|h|\leq H with

(6.9) H:=P​x−1+δ,H:=Px^{-1+\delta},

as before. Then, one removed the smooth cross-conditions in h,m,nh,m,n, and separated k=(m,n)k=(m,n) to reach the type-II sums Σk​(M,N)\Sigma_{k}(M,N) from the first display on [37, p. 1275]; we need to bound these by ≪εx1−δ/k\ll_{\varepsilon}x^{1-\delta}/k, for δ=δ⁡(ε)\delta=\delta(\varepsilon) to be chosen.

In [37, §3.5], one applied Cauchy–Schwarz keeping the sums over h,nh,n inside, to obtain

(6.10) Σk​(M,N)≪(Mk)1/2​Ξk​(M,N)1/2,\Sigma_{k}(M,N)\ll\left(\frac{M}{k}\right)^{1/2}\Xi_{k}(M,N)^{1/2},

and trivially bounded the contribution of h2​n1=h1​n2h_{2}n_{1}=h_{1}n_{2} to Ξk\Xi_{k}, using the condition N≫εxα−1+εN\gg_{\varepsilon}x^{\alpha-1+\varepsilon}; then they separated n0=(n1,n2)n_{0}=(n_{1},n_{2}) (and let ni←ni/n0n_{i}\leftarrow n_{i}/n_{0}). We note that considering nontrivial values of the GCD-parameters kk and n0n_{0} was not necessary in the proof of Proposition 22.(i​i)(ii), since then (bn)(b_{n}) was supported on primes; in a first pass the reader can pretend that k=n0=1k=n_{0}=1.

In [37, §3.6], one expanded the condition (m,n0​n1​n2)=1(m,n_{0}n_{1}n_{2})=1 by Möbius inversion, resulting in a sum over d|n0​n1​n2d\mid n_{0}n_{1}n_{2} (we switched notation from δ\delta to dd). Then, one applied Gauss’ lemma ([37, Lemma 9]), resulting in sums Ψk​(R,S)\Psi_{k}(R,S) of incomplete Kloosterman sums, ranging over r,sr,s of sizes

(6.11) 1≪R,S≪P​Nk​n0.1\ll R,S\ll\sqrt{\frac{PN}{kn_{0}}}.

In [37, §3.7], one completed Kloosterman sums, resulting in a sum over |t|≤T|t|\leq T with

and trivially bounded the contribution of t=0t=0. This ultimately leads to the sums of Kloosterman sums Ψ~k​(R,S)\widetilde{\Psi}_{k}(R,S) from [37, p. 1279], which have a relevant level of

(6.13) ϱ:=d​k2​n0​n1​n2≍d​N2n0.\varrho:=dk^{2}n_{0}n_{1}n_{2}\asymp\frac{dN^{2}}{n_{0}}.

Finally, in [37, §3.8], Merikoski used [10, Theorem 9] to bound the trilinear sums of Kloosterman sums

𝒦=𝒦⁡(d,n0,n1,n2):=maxα⁡(mod ​ϱ)⁡|∑m∼ℳam​∑n∼𝒩bn​∑(c,ϱ)=1Φ⁡(mℳ,n𝒩,c𝒞)​S​(m​ϱ¯,±n,c)|,\mathcal{K}=\mathcal{K}(d,n_{0},n_{1},n_{2}):=\max_{\alpha\ (\textnormal{mod }\varrho)}\left|\sum_{m\sim\mathcal{M}}a_{m}\sum_{n\sim\mathcal{N}}b_{n}\sum_{(c,\varrho)=1}\Phi\left(\frac{m}{\mathcal{M}},\frac{n}{\mathcal{N}},\frac{c}{\mathcal{C}}\right)S\left(m\overline{\varrho},\pm n;c\right)\right|,

where Φ\Phi is a smooth function as in Corollary 16 with Z=1Z=1, (ch)(c_{h}) are bounded coefficients,

(6.15) ℳ≪T,𝒩≪H​Nk​n0,𝒞≪S,\mathcal{M}\ll T,\qquad\qquad\mathcal{N}\ll\frac{HN}{kn_{0}},\qquad\qquad\mathcal{C}\ll S,

To do so, we note that the coefficients chc_{h} (obtained by removing the cross-condition in h,m,nh,m,n on [37, p. 1274]) are smooth functions of hh. In fact, expanding |𝒜m​n|−ρ⁡(m​n)m​n|\mathcal{A}_{mn}|-\frac{\rho(mn)}{mn} via Lemma 4 and fixing j,uj,u up to a logarithmic loss, we can use the coefficients

from 3.4, where 1≤2j=Hj≤H=P​x−1+δ1\leq 2^{j}=H_{j}\leq H=Px^{-1+\delta}, u≍1u\asymp 1, and Ψj:(12,2)→ℂ\Psi_{j}:(\frac{1}{2},2)\to\mathbb{C} are compactly-supported smooth functions with bounded derivatives. 6.3. Sieve computations

To complete the proof of Theorem 1, it remains to adapt the calculation in [37, §2] with our Type I and Type II information.

In the expression for G5G_{5}, we implicitly used the value D=x1/2−εD=x^{1/2-\varepsilon} since 12<(1−2​θ​α)2−5​θ\frac{1}{2}<\frac{(1-2\theta\alpha)}{2-5\theta} for α≤139/114\alpha\leq 139/114, and the fact that 1<1/(2​(α−1))≤31<1/(2(\alpha-1))\leq 3 for 7/6≤α≤139/1147/6\leq\alpha\leq 139/114. Thus

∑x≤P≤x139/114P=2j​xS⁡(x,P)<0.59097​X​log⁡x.\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}x\leq P\leq x^{139/114}\\ P=2^{j}x\end{subarray}}S(x,P)<0.59097\,X\log x.

For the remaining range α≥139/114\alpha\geq 139/114, we apply Lemma 24 to obtain (as in [37, (2.8)])

∑x139/114≤P≤xω¯P=2j​xS⁡(x,P)≤(4​∫139/1141.25α​𝑑α+(4−10​θ)​∫1.25ω¯α1−2​θ​α​𝑑α)​X​log⁡x,\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}x^{139/114}\leq P\leq x^{\overline{\omega}}\\ P=2^{j}x\end{subarray}}S(x,P)\leq\left(4\int_{139/114}^{1.25}\alpha\,d\alpha+(4-10\theta)\int_{1.25}^{\overline{\omega}}\frac{\alpha}{1-2\theta\alpha}d\alpha\right)X\log x,

where α=1.25=5/4\alpha=1.25=5/4 is the threshold at which the expression for DD changes (i.e., when 12=(1−2​θ​α)2−5​θ\frac{1}{2}=\frac{(1-2\theta\alpha)}{2-5\theta}). We conclude that 6.20 holds (for small enough ε\varepsilon) provided that

(4−10​θ)​∫1.25ω¯α1−2​θ​α​𝑑α<1−0.59097−4​∫139/1141.25α​𝑑α,(4-10\theta)\int_{1.25}^{\overline{\omega}}\frac{\alpha}{1-2\theta\alpha}d\alpha<1-0.59097-4\int_{139/114}^{1.25}\alpha\,d\alpha,

where the right-hand side is at least 0.2574060.257406. This inequality (barely) holds true when ω¯=1.30008\overline{\omega}=1.30008, which proves Theorem 1. ∎
